Torsades de pointes
content: Cardiac arrhythmias encompass a broad spectrum of abnormal heart rhythms ranging from benign ectopics to immediately life-threatening ventricular fibrillation. Emergency assessment requires systematic evaluation of haemodynamic stability, the nature of the arrhythmia (tachyarrhythmia versus bradyarrhythmia), QRS duration (narrow versus wide), and patient symptoms including palpitations, chest pain, dyspnoea, pre-syncope, or syncope. All patients presenting with arrhythmia should have a 12-lead ECG, continuous cardiac monitoring, blood pressure measurement, SpO2, and serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium), thyroid function, and cardiac biomarkers. Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is the most common paroxysmal tachyarrhythmia in otherwise healthy individuals, presenting with sudden-onset palpitations and heart rate typically between 150–250 bpm with a narrow QRS complex. Vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, modified Valsalva, carotid sinus massage in patients over 40 without carotid bruit) should be attempted first. Intravenous adenosine (6 mg, repeated as 12 mg) is first-line pharmacological therapy. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia and must be classified by duration (paroxysmal, persistent, permanent) for therapeutic decision-making around rate versus rhythm control and anticoagulation. Haemodynamically unstable AF requires immediate synchronised DC cardioversion. Rate control agents include beta-blockers and rate-limiting calcium channel blockers. All patients with AF should have CHA₂DS₂-VASc and HAS-BLED scores calculated to guide anticoagulation decisions. Ventricular tachycardia (VT) with a pulse and haemodynamic stability may respond to IV amiodarone; pulseless VT and VF require immediate defibrillation and advanced cardiac life support. Complete heart block presenting with haemodynamic compromise requires urgent transcutaneous pacing followed by transvenous pacing while awaiting permanent pacemaker implantation.

title: Peripheral Neuropathy: Assessment, Causes and Referral Guidance
red_flags: Rapidly ascending weakness (Guillain-Barré)
Autonomic dysfunction (urinary retention, orthostasis)
Severe pain with respiratory compromise
Cranial nerve involvement with peripheral neuropathy
content: Peripheral neuropathy refers to damage or dysfunction of the peripheral nervous system, encompassing motor, sensory, and autonomic nerves. It may affect a single nerve (mononeuropathy), multiple isolated nerves (mononeuritis multiplex), or diffuse nerve fibres (polyneuropathy). The most common underlying cause in the United Kingdom is diabetes mellitus, responsible for approximately one-third of all cases of peripheral polyneuropathy; other frequent causes include alcohol excess, vitamin B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, paraproteinaemia, and hereditary conditions such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Symptoms vary with the type and distribution of nerve fibres involved: sensory involvement produces numbness, tingling, burning dysaesthesia, or loss of proprioception; motor involvement causes distal weakness and muscle wasting; autonomic involvement may manifest as postural hypotension, abnormal sweating, erectile dysfunction, or gastroparesis. The length-dependent pattern — beginning in the feet and ascending proximally — is characteristic of metabolic and toxic neuropathies. Assessment should include a comprehensive neurological examination documenting tendon reflexes, muscle strength, vibration and pin-prick sensation, proprioception, and gait. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography (NCS/EMG) provide electrophysiological characterisation, distinguishing axonal from demyelinating pathology. Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) — an acute immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy — must be recognised promptly: progressive ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia following a gastrointestinal or respiratory infection, with potential respiratory involvement requiring ICU admission, warrants immediate hospitalisation. Blood investigations should include HbA1c, vitamin B12, folate, TFTs, FBC, ESR, LFTs, paraprotein screen, and HIV testing where indicated. Lumbar puncture may be required in suspected inflammatory or infective neuropathy. Treatment is directed at the underlying cause. Pain management for neuropathic pain should follow NICE guidance: amitriptyline, duloxetine, pregabalin, or gabapentin are first-line agents. Referral to neurology is recommended for undiagnosed neuropathy, rapidly progressive symptoms, significant motor involvement, or suspected inflammatory aetiology.

title: Cluster Headache: Diagnosis, Acute Treatment and Preventive Management

content: Cluster headache is one of the most severe pain conditions known in medicine, often described by patients as the worst pain they have ever experienced. It is classified under trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs) and is characterised by attacks of unilateral, strictly orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain of excruciating severity, lasting 15–180 minutes, occurring from once every other day to eight times daily. Associated ipsilateral autonomic features are pathognomonic: conjunctival injection and lacrimation, nasal congestion or rhinorrhoea, eyelid oedema, miosis, and ptosis (Horner's syndrome). Unlike migraineurs who prefer to lie still, cluster headache patients are typically agitated and restless during attacks. Attacks occur in bouts or 'clusters' lasting weeks to months, separated by pain-free remission periods, though a minority of patients develop chronic cluster headache without remission. The diagnosis is clinical, based on International Headache Society (IHS) criteria. Secondary causes must be excluded: pituitary adenoma, arteriovenous malformation, and cavernous sinus pathology may mimic cluster headache and should prompt neuroimaging with pituitary-protocol MRI and MRA. Acute treatment options include high-flow oxygen (100%, 12–15 L/min via non-rebreather mask for 15–20 minutes), which is effective in approximately 70% of attacks, and subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg (maximum two doses in 24 hours), which is the most rapidly effective pharmacological treatment. Intranasal zolmitriptan is an alternative when injection is not acceptable. Preventive therapy is essential and should be initiated at the onset of each cluster period: verapamil (starting dose 240 mg, titrated to 480 mg or higher in divided doses) is the drug of choice. Short-term prevention with a tapering course of oral prednisolone (60 mg reducing over three weeks) may be used to bridge the latency period before verapamil takes effect. Greater occipital nerve blocks provide rapid short-term relief. Patients not responding to these measures should be referred to a tertiary headache clinic for consideration of monoclonal anti-CGRP antibodies (galcanezumab) or neurostimulation (sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation, vagus nerve stimulation).

title: Cervical Myelopathy: Recognition, Urgency of Referral and Surgical Indications
red_flags: Acute deterioration with quadriparesis
Bladder or bowel dysfunction with myelopathic signs
Bilateral upper limb weakness and spasticity

content: Cervical myelopathy is a clinical syndrome resulting from compression of the spinal cord within the cervical vertebral canal, most commonly due to degenerative cervical spondylosis with osteophyte formation, disc herniation, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, or ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL). It is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults over fifty years of age. The clinical presentation is characteristically insidious and progressive, beginning with gait disturbance — broad-based, unsteady, spastic gait — difficulty with fine motor tasks such as handwriting and buttoning, and bilateral upper limb numbness and tingling. Significant features include upper motor neurone signs in the lower limbs (hyperreflexia, ankle clonus, extensor plantar response), loss of proprioception and vibration sensation, and in advanced cases, bladder or bowel dysfunction indicating severe cord compromise. Lhermitte's sign — an electric shock sensation radiating down the spine or limbs on neck flexion — is a highly characteristic feature of posterior column involvement. Assessment using validated tools such as the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score (0–18, with 18 indicating normal function) allows classification of severity: mild (15–17), moderate (12–14), and severe (<12). MRI of the cervical spine is the investigation of choice and may demonstrate cord signal change on T2 (hyperintensity), indicating intrinsic cord damage and predicting poorer surgical outcome. Myelopathy in the context of acute trauma, significant instability, or rapidly progressive neurological deterioration requires urgent neurosurgical assessment. For moderate-to-severe myelopathy, surgical decompression — anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF), anterior corpectomy, or posterior laminoplasty/laminectomy — halts progression and may allow partial neurological recovery in a majority of patients. Conservative management with cervical collar and physiotherapy may be considered for mild cases with stable symptoms, but requires close monitoring.

title: Viral Encephalitis: Emergency Diagnosis and Empirical Treatment

Decreased level of consciousness

content: Viral encephalitis is a medical emergency defined as acute inflammation of the brain parenchyma, most commonly caused by Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), which accounts for the majority of sporadic cases in the developed world and carries a mortality exceeding 70% if untreated. Other important causative agents include Varicella zoster virus (VZV), enteroviruses, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Japanese encephalitis virus in endemic regions. The clinical triad of fever, headache, and altered mental status is the cardinal presentation, often accompanied by personality or behavioural changes (particularly prominent in HSV-1 encephalitis due to its predilection for the temporal and orbitofrontal cortices), focal neurological signs, and seizures. Prodromal symptoms may include respiratory or gastrointestinal illness preceding neurological onset by days. Emergency management must not be delayed pending investigation results. Empirical intravenous aciclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) should be started immediately in any patient with suspected encephalitis, prior to CT and lumbar puncture, as delay worsens outcome. CT brain should precede lumbar puncture to exclude raised intracranial pressure (papilloedema, mass lesion, or midline shift). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and normal or mildly reduced glucose. HSV PCR on CSF is the diagnostic gold standard with sensitivity exceeding 95%. MRI brain (T2/FLAIR) shows characteristic hyperintensity in the temporal lobes and insular cortex in HSV-1 encephalitis. EEG may demonstrate periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) or diffuse slow-wave activity. Autoimmune encephalitis — particularly anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis — must be considered in younger patients with prominent psychiatric features, movement disorders, autonomic instability, and seizures; this requires CSF and serum antibody testing and immunotherapy. Aciclovir should be continued for 14–21 days. Patients should be managed in a high-dependency or neurological intensive care unit.

title: Sudden Visual Loss: Urgent Assessment and Ophthalmological Referral

content: Sudden visual loss is a neurological and ophthalmological emergency requiring urgent assessment to identify and treat potentially reversible or life-threatening causes. It encompasses monocular visual loss — suggesting pathology anterior to the optic chiasm — and binocular or hemianopic visual loss — indicating retrochiasmal pathology. Painless monocular visual loss in older adults must immediately raise suspicion for central or branch retinal artery occlusion (CRAO/BRAO), which carries a visual prognosis similar to ischaemic stroke and represents a true ophthalmic emergency. CRAO presents with sudden, painless, complete or near-complete loss of vision in one eye; fundoscopy classically reveals retinal pallor with a cherry-red spot at the fovea. Time-sensitive interventions — lowering intraocular pressure, ocular massage, anterior chamber paracentesis, and hyperbaric oxygen — may be attempted within four to six hours of onset, though evidence remains limited. All patients with CRAO must be assessed for cardiovascular risk factors and undergo rapid TIA workup including carotid Doppler, echocardiography, and embolic source investigation. Giant cell arteritis (GCA) must be excluded in patients over 50 with sudden visual loss associated with headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, proximal myalgia (polymyalgia rheumatica), elevated ESR (>50 mm/hr), and CRP. Vision loss in GCA is caused by anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION) from ophthalmic artery vasculitis; oral prednisolone 60 mg daily must be started immediately without awaiting temporal artery biopsy, as the other eye is at risk within hours to days. Sudden visual loss in young adults should raise suspicion for optic neuritis associated with multiple sclerosis: typically unilateral, painful (worsened by eye movement), and associated with central visual field loss and reduced colour saturation. MRI brain and orbits with gadolinium should be obtained urgently. Amaurosis fugax — transient monocular visual loss lasting seconds to minutes — is a TIA equivalent and demands immediate vascular assessment.

title: Parkinson's Disease: Diagnosis, Referral and Early Management

content: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer's disease, affecting approximately 145,000 people in the United Kingdom. It results from progressive degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and widespread Lewy body pathology. The diagnosis is clinical, based on the cardinal motor features: bradykinesia (essential for diagnosis) plus at least one of resting tremor (4–6 Hz, characteristically pill-rolling, suppressed by voluntary movement), rigidity (cogwheel or lead-pipe), and postural instability. Non-motor features — often preceding motor symptoms by years — include anosmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression, and autonomic dysfunction. The UK Parkinson's Disease Brain Bank criteria are the established diagnostic standard. Clinicians must distinguish idiopathic PD from atypical Parkinsonian syndromes: progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) presents with early falls, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, and axial rigidity; multiple system atrophy (MSA) with prominent autonomic failure; dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) with early cognitive fluctuations, visual hallucinations, and REM sleep behaviour disorder. Atypical features — symmetrical onset, early severe postural instability, absent tremor, early dementia, early autonomic failure, rapid progression — mandate urgent neurological review and DAT-SPECT imaging to confirm dopaminergic deficit. Levodopa remains the most effective symptomatic therapy for motor features and is typically started in combination with a peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor (co-careldopa or co-beneldopa). Dopamine agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole) are alternatives in younger patients. Referral to a specialist Parkinson's nurse and multidisciplinary team (physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy) is essential from diagnosis. All patients with new or suspected Parkinson's disease should be referred to a consultant neurologist with special interest in movement disorders. Advanced therapies — DBS, apomorphine pump, levodopa-entacapone-carbidopa intestinal gel — should be considered when motor complications arise.

title: Early Cognitive Impairment and Suspected Dementia: Assessment and Referral

content: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represents the transitional state between normal age-related cognitive changes and dementia, characterised by objective cognitive decline in one or more domains that does not significantly impair daily functional activities. Dementia is defined as a syndrome of progressive cognitive decline — affecting memory, language, executive function, attention, and visuospatial abilities — severe enough to interfere with daily life and social functioning. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause (60–70%), followed by vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, and frontotemporal dementia. Initial assessment in primary care should include a structured cognitive screening tool (MMSE, Montreal Cognitive Assessment — MoCA, or Mini-Cog), collateral history from a carer, medication review for anticholinergic burden, and assessment for reversible causes. Reversible and treatable causes of cognitive impairment that must be excluded include hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, hypo- or hypernatraemia, hepatic or renal encephalopathy, depression (pseudo-dementia), NPH (normal pressure hydrocephalus — triad of dementia, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence), intracranial mass lesion, and subdural haematoma. Standard investigations include FBC, U&E, TFTs, B12, folate, glucose, LFTs, calcium, and urinalysis. Brain imaging (CT or preferably MRI) should be performed to exclude structural causes and characterise atrophy patterns. Rapid progressive dementia (<6 months), myoclonus, cerebellar signs, or early behavioural change should prompt urgent referral for prion disease investigation including CSF 14-3-3 protein and RT-QuIC. All patients with suspected dementia should be referred to a memory clinic or old age psychiatry for formal neuropsychological assessment, specialist diagnosis, and care planning. Anticholinergic medications, benzodiazepines, and other cognitive-impairing drugs should be reviewed and minimised. Advance care planning should be initiated early while the patient retains capacity.

title: Trigeminal Neuralgia and Facial Pain Disorders: Differential Diagnosis and Treatment

content: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is a severe, paroxysmal facial pain disorder characterised by brief, electric shock-like or stabbing attacks of intense unilateral pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve (V2 and V3 most commonly). Attacks are typically triggered by light touch to trigger zones — eating, talking, brushing teeth, shaving, or exposure to cold — and last from a fraction of a second to two minutes. Classical TN is caused by neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root, most commonly by the superior cerebellar artery. Secondary TN — associated with multiple sclerosis, cerebellopontine angle tumours (acoustic neuroma, meningioma), or skull base lesions — must be excluded, particularly in younger patients, bilateral presentations, or when neurological examination reveals objective sensory loss. Idiopathic TN is a diagnosis of exclusion. MRI brain with high-resolution sequences through the posterior fossa (CISS or FIESTA) is required in all patients to identify neurovascular contact and exclude secondary causes. The differential diagnosis of facial pain is broad and includes atypical facial pain (persistent idiopathic facial pain), temporomandibular joint dysfunction, dental pathology, cluster headache, SUNCT (short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with conjunctival injection and tearing), postherpetic neuralgia following VZV, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. First-line pharmacological treatment is carbamazepine (100–200 mg twice daily, titrated to response), which achieves pain control in 70–80% of patients. Oxcarbazepine is an alternative with a better tolerability profile. Lamotrigine and gabapentin may be used in refractory or carbamazepine-intolerant patients. Surgical options for medically refractory TN include microvascular decompression (MVD) — the most durable intervention, particularly effective for classical TN with demonstrated neurovascular conflict — percutaneous rhizotomy techniques, and stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife). Referral to a neurosurgeon or specialist neurology pain clinic is recommended for all patients not achieving adequate pain control with carbamazepine.

title: Sleep Disorders: Assessment of Insomnia, Narcolepsy and Parasomnias
red_flags: Excessive daytime somnolence with cataplexy (narcolepsy)

content: Sleep disorders represent a diverse group of conditions that adversely affect sleep quality, timing, and duration, with significant downstream consequences for cognitive performance, cardiovascular health, metabolic regulation, and mental wellbeing. Chronic insomnia disorder — defined as difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep occurring at least three nights per week for more than three months — affects approximately 10–15% of the adult population. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the evidence-based first-line treatment and is superior to pharmacotherapy in the long term. Sleep hygiene education, stimulus control, sleep restriction therapy, and relaxation techniques are core CBT-I components. Pharmacological options — benzodiazepines, Z-drugs (zopiclone, zolpidem), doxepin, and melatonin — should be used sparingly and for limited durations due to dependency risk and adverse cognitive effects. Narcolepsy is a chronic neurological disorder of sleep-wake regulation caused by loss of hypocretin (orexin)-producing neurons in the hypothalamus, resulting in excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions), hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis. Diagnosis requires polysomnography followed by multiple sleep latency testing (MSLT) demonstrating a mean sleep onset latency of less than eight minutes with two or more sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs). CSF hypocretin measurement is diagnostic when below 110 pg/mL. REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) — acting out vivid dreams due to loss of REM sleep atonia — is a prodromal synucleinopathy marker: over 80% of patients with idiopathic RBD develop Parkinson's disease, MSA, or DLB within 10–15 years, warranting specialist follow-up. Parasomnias including sleepwalking, sleep terrors, and confusional arousals occur during NREM sleep and are managed with safety counselling and scheduled awakening. All complex sleep disorders should be evaluated at a sleep centre with attended polysomnography.

title: Orbital Cellulitis and Retro-Orbital Pathology: Emergency Recognition and Management

content: Orbital cellulitis is a serious bacterial infection of the soft tissues of the orbit posterior to the orbital septum, representing a potential sight- and life-threatening emergency. It must be distinguished from preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis, which is confined anterior to the orbital septum and carries a considerably better prognosis. The distinction is critical: preseptal cellulitis presents with eyelid erythema, oedema, and warmth without ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, or pain on eye movement; orbital cellulitis produces the additional features of proptosis, restricted and painful extraocular movements, chemosis, and potentially reduced visual acuity. Orbital cellulitis most commonly arises as a complication of acute sinusitis — particularly ethmoid sinusitis — with direct spread of bacterial infection through the thin lamina papyracea. Common causative organisms include Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), Streptococcus species, Haemophilus influenzae, and mixed anaerobes. CT orbits with contrast is the investigation of choice and can identify subperiosteal or orbital abscess requiring surgical drainage. Cavernous sinus thrombosis — a severe and potentially fatal complication — presents with bilateral proptosis, bilateral ophthalmoplegia, high fever, severe headache, signs of meningeal irritation, and septic features. MRI with MRV is diagnostic for cavernous sinus thrombosis. Management of orbital cellulitis requires urgent hospital admission, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone with metronidazole), and close monitoring of visual acuity, pupillary responses, and eye movement every two to four hours. Surgical drainage of abscess — endoscopic endonasal or external orbital approach — is indicated for large subperiosteal abscesses, vision-threatening disease, failure to improve within 24–48 hours, or cavernous sinus involvement. Ophthalmology, ENT, and infectious disease teams should be involved from presentation. Systemic anticoagulation is debated in cavernous sinus thrombosis but may be considered in selected cases.

title: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension: Diagnosis, Vision Monitoring and Treatment
red_flags: Rapid loss of visual field (peripheral constriction)
Papilloedema with visual acuity loss
Sixth cranial nerve palsy with headache
Severe positional headache with vomiting
content: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), previously termed pseudotumour cerebri, is a disorder of elevated intracranial pressure in the absence of an identifiable causative intracranial pathology. It predominantly affects obese women of childbearing age, with an incidence that has risen in parallel with obesity prevalence. The hallmark presentation is a daily, persistent, often postural headache — typically worse in the morning or with Valsalva manoeuvres — associated with pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations (brief dimming or greying of vision lasting seconds, particularly on positional change), diplopia from sixth cranial nerve palsy, and visual field defects. Papilloedema is present in the majority of cases and may be bilateral and asymmetric; its absence does not exclude IIH. Critically, visual field loss is the major source of permanent morbidity and may be irreversible if the condition is not treated promptly. The modified Dandy criteria for diagnosis require: clinical features consistent with raised ICP; exclusion of secondary causes by neuroimaging (MRI brain and MRV to exclude venous sinus thrombosis, intracranial mass, hydrocephalus, and meningeal infiltration); elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture (>25 cmH₂O in a relaxed lateral decubitus position); normal CSF composition; and no other identifiable cause. MRI signs may include flattening of the posterior globes, optic nerve sheath distension, and empty sella. Management aims to reduce ICP, control headache, and preserve vision. Weight loss of 5–10% is highly effective in improving both symptoms and papilloedema in overweight patients. First-line pharmacological treatment is acetazolamide (500 mg to 2 g daily in divided doses), a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production. Regular visual field monitoring with Humphrey perimetry and assessment of papilloedema by optical coherence tomography (OCT) are mandatory. Surgical interventions — CSF diversion via ventriculoperitoneal or lumboperitoneal shunt, or optic nerve sheath fenestration — are reserved for cases with refractory vision loss.

title: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss: Urgent Investigation and Treatment
red_flags: Sudden unilateral deafness with vertigo (neurovascular emergency)
Bilateral sudden hearing loss
Sudden hearing loss with focal neurological signs (posterior fossa stroke)
Hearing loss with aural fullness and new facial weakness
content: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) is defined as a sensorineural hearing loss of 30 dB or greater across three consecutive frequencies, occurring within 72 hours. It is a medical emergency with important implications for hearing preservation and must be managed urgently, as the prognosis for spontaneous recovery or treatment-induced improvement declines significantly with delayed intervention. SSNHL has an incidence of 5–27 per 100,000 per year and is estimated to be idiopathic in 85–90% of cases. Proposed aetiologies for idiopathic SSNHL include viral infection (mumps, CMV, herpes viruses), vascular ischaemia of the cochlear or vestibulocochlear nerve supply, membrane rupture (perilymph fistula), and immune-mediated cochlear damage. Clinicians must exclude structural and vascular causes before attributing SSNHL to an idiopathic aetiology: MRI of the internal auditory canal (IAC) and posterior fossa with gadolinium is essential to exclude acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma), which presents in approximately 10% of SSNHL cases, as well as meningioma, intralabyrinthine haemorrhage, MS, and posterior fossa stroke. Pure-tone audiometry is required to characterise the degree and configuration of hearing loss. Autoimmune conditions — including Cogan's syndrome and systemic lupus — may cause bilateral SSNHL and should be screened for. Standard treatment is a course of systemic corticosteroids: oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg) for 7–14 days with taper. Intratympanic dexamethasone injection — as primary therapy or as salvage treatment — delivers high local drug concentrations to the cochlea with minimal systemic side effects. Treatment should be initiated ideally within 72 hours of onset, with a maximum benefit window of two to four weeks. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be considered as an adjunct. All patients should be managed by an ENT specialist, with audiology rehabilitation (hearing aids, cochlear implant assessment if profound loss) if recovery is incomplete.

title: Epilepsy Management in Low-Resource Settings: Global Guidance on Diagnosis and Treatment
red_flags: Status epilepticus (seizure >5 minutes or recurrent without recovery)
New-onset seizure with fever and meningism (meningitis)
Seizure with postictal focal deficit (Todd's paralysis, Todd's aphasia)
First seizure in pregnancy (eclampsia)
content: Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, making it one of the most common serious neurological disorders globally. The WHO mhGAP (Mental Health Gap Action Programme) intervention guide provides evidence-based recommendations for the management of epilepsy in non-specialist health settings, particularly relevant to low- and middle-income countries where the treatment gap — the proportion of people with epilepsy who do not receive appropriate treatment — may exceed 75%. Epilepsy is defined as at least two unprovoked seizures occurring more than 24 hours apart, or one unprovoked seizure with a high probability of recurrence. Seizures are classified into focal (arising from a localised network in one hemisphere), generalised (involving both hemispheres from onset), or unknown onset. Clinicians must distinguish epileptic seizures from non-epileptic events including syncope, psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES), hypoglycaemia, transient ischaemic attacks, and migrainous aura. Provoked acute seizures — caused by hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, drug or alcohol withdrawal, CNS infection, or head trauma — require treatment of the underlying cause rather than antiepileptic medication. EEG and neuroimaging (CT or MRI) are essential for seizure classification and identification of structural causes. First-line antiepileptic drugs recommended by WHO include phenobarbital (inexpensive, effective, widely available), carbamazepine (focal seizures), valproate (generalised seizures, noting teratogenicity in women of childbearing potential), and phenytoin. Status epilepticus — defined as a seizure lasting more than five minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness — is a neurological emergency with mortality exceeding 20% and requires immediate benzodiazepine administration (diazepam 10 mg IV or rectally, lorazepam 4 mg IV), followed by levetiracetam, phenytoin, or valproate if initial therapy fails. Second-line benzodiazepine resistance should prompt anaesthetic coma. All patients with new-onset seizures should undergo specialist neurology review.

title: Meningitis in Children: Global Emergency Recognition and Treatment Standards
red_flags: Non-blanching petechial rash with fever (meningococcaemia)
Bulging fontanelle in infants
Triad of fever, headache, and neck stiffness
Altered consciousness with papilloedema
content: Bacterial meningitis remains a major cause of childhood mortality and neurological disability worldwide, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and South and East Asia. The WHO global strategy for defeating meningitis by 2030 targets the elimination of bacterial meningitis as a public health threat through improved vaccination coverage, rapid diagnosis, and timely treatment. The classic clinical triad of bacterial meningitis — fever, headache, and neck stiffness — is present in only 44% of adult cases; in infants and young children the presentation may be non-specific, including high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, refusal to feed, photophobia, irritability, and seizures. Kernig's sign (inability to extend the knee with the hip flexed) and Brudzinski's sign (involuntary hip flexion on passive neck flexion) indicate meningeal irritation. The most feared complication is meningococcal septicaemia (Neisseria meningitidis), which may progress within hours from initial fever to fulminant septicaemic shock and death; non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash is the clinical hallmark and demands immediate parenteral benzylpenicillin (or ceftriaxone) administration without delay, even before hospital transfer. LP should not be performed if there are signs of raised ICP, coagulopathy, or haemodynamic instability. CSF findings in bacterial meningitis include turbid appearance, elevated opening pressure, neutrophilic pleocytosis (>100 cells/mm³), elevated protein (>0.45 g/L), markedly reduced glucose (<40 mg/dL, CSF:serum ratio <0.4), and positive Gram stain and culture. Empirical antibiotic therapy should cover Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis (ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day) with ampicillin added for Listeria in neonates and immunocompromised patients. Dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg 6-hourly for four days) reduces the risk of severe neurological sequelae including hearing loss in children with pneumococcal meningitis. Routine vaccination programmes (MenB, MenACWY, pneumococcal, Hib) are the cornerstone of prevention.

title: Stroke and Cerebrovascular Disease: Global Management and Secondary Prevention
red_flags: Sudden facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty (FAST positive)
Sudden severe headache (worst ever — subarachnoid haemorrhage)
Sudden loss of vision or vertigo with ataxia (posterior circulation stroke)
Acute hemiplegia with hypertensive crisis
content: Stroke is the second leading cause of death and the third leading cause of disability globally, according to the World Health Organization. The WHO action plan for stroke prevention and control emphasises early recognition, timely reperfusion therapy, integrated stroke unit care, and secondary prevention as the four pillars of stroke management. Stroke is classified as ischaemic (87% of cases) — caused by thrombotic or embolic arterial occlusion — or haemorrhagic (13%) — resulting from intracerebral haemorrhage or subarachnoid haemorrhage. The FAST acronym (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services) is the global public awareness tool. Time is critical: for ischaemic stroke, intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA, alteplase) must be administered within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, and mechanical thrombectomy extends the treatment window to 6–24 hours for selected patients with large vessel occlusion. All patients with suspected stroke should be assessed in a hyperacute stroke unit with immediate non-contrast CT brain to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis. CT angiography identifies large vessel occlusion for thrombectomy candidacy. MRI brain (DWI sequence) detects acute ischaemia with higher sensitivity than CT. Atrial fibrillation is identified in 20–30% of stroke patients through cardiac monitoring and requires anticoagulation for secondary prevention. Carotid stenosis above 50% in symptomatic patients is an indication for carotid endarterectomy or stenting. Following acute treatment, all stroke patients require comprehensive rehabilitation — physiotherapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy — in a stroke unit setting, which independently reduces mortality and disability compared to general medical wards. Secondary prevention includes antiplatelets for non-cardioembolic stroke, risk factor management (hypertension, diabetes, lipids, smoking cessation), and lifestyle modification.

title: Mental Health Disorders and Neurological Comorbidity: WHO Global Management Framework
red_flags: Active suicidal ideation with neurological comorbidity
Sudden behavioural change with confusion (organic cause)
Psychosis in context of systemic disease (secondary)
Severe agitation with new neurological signs
content: Neuropsychiatric disorders — encompassing conditions at the interface of neurology and psychiatry — represent a significant and growing global health burden. The WHO integrated framework for neurological and mental health conditions highlights that many brain disorders present simultaneously with both neurological and psychiatric features, and that artificial separation of mind and brain disorders delays appropriate diagnosis and care. Depression is two to three times more prevalent in patients with neurological conditions (epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, MS, stroke, TBI) than in the general population and independently worsens neurological outcomes, quality of life, and adherence to treatment. Anxiety disorders are equally prevalent and frequently underdiagnosed. Clinicians caring for patients with neurological conditions should routinely screen for depression and anxiety using validated tools: PHQ-9, GAD-7, or neurological-specific tools such as the Neurological Disorders Depression Inventory for Epilepsy (NDDI-E). Psychosis may arise secondary to neurological conditions (epilepsy-related psychosis, anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, limbic encephalitis, Lewy body dementia) or as a side effect of neurological medications (levodopa, corticosteroids, antiepileptics). New-onset psychosis with cognitive impairment, fever, movement disorder, or abnormal CSF/EEG/MRI should prompt thorough investigation for autoimmune, infective, or structural CNS causes before a primary psychiatric diagnosis is made. Delirium — characterised by acute fluctuating disturbance in attention and awareness — is a neuropsychiatric syndrome and must be distinguished from primary psychiatric disease; it carries significant mortality risk in hospitalised patients. Multidisciplinary collaboration between neurology, psychiatry, and primary care is essential for optimal management of neuropsychiatric comorbidity. The WHO mhGAP guidelines provide evidence-based treatment recommendations adaptable to low-resource settings, including pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions for depression, psychosis, and epilepsy.

title: Ascites: Assessment, Differential Diagnosis and Management
red_flags: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever with ascites)
Tense ascites with respiratory compromise
Rapidly reaccumulating ascites (malignant cause)
Encephalopathy with ascites (decompensated cirrhosis)
content: Ascites is defined as the pathological accumulation of fluid within the peritoneal cavity and represents the most common complication of liver cirrhosis, accounting for approximately 75% of cases. Other causes include malignant ascites (peritoneal carcinomatosis or hepatocellular carcinoma), cardiac failure, constrictive pericarditis, nephrotic syndrome, tuberculosis, and Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic venous outflow obstruction). The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is the most reliable initial diagnostic test to classify ascites: a SAAG ≥11 g/L indicates portal hypertension (cirrhosis, cardiac failure, Budd-Chiari), while SAAG <11 g/L suggests non-portal-hypertensive aetiology (malignancy, tuberculosis, nephrotic syndrome). Clinical assessment should determine fluid volume (shifting dullness, fluid thrill), nutritional status, and the presence of stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, Dupuytren's contracture, hepatic encephalopathy). Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid analysis — cell count and differential, protein, albumin, LDH, glucose, culture, cytology, and ADA if tuberculosis is suspected — is mandatory for new-onset ascites or clinical deterioration. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) must be excluded when cirrhotic patients with ascites develop fever, abdominal pain, or encephalopathy: ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ is diagnostic and warrants immediate empirical antibiotics (cefotaxime or tazobactam) and 20% albumin infusion to prevent hepatorenal syndrome. First-line management of cirrhotic ascites includes dietary sodium restriction (<90 mmol/day), spironolactone (starting 100 mg daily, titrated up to 400 mg), and furosemide (starting 40 mg daily). Refractory ascites unresponsive to maximal diuretic therapy requires serial large-volume paracentesis with concurrent albumin infusion (8 g per litre of ascites drained), or transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) insertion in selected patients. Liver transplantation should be considered for eligible patients with decompensated cirrhosis.

title: Small Bowel Obstruction: Clinical Assessment, Imaging and Surgical Indications
red_flags: Signs of strangulation (peritonism, fever, tachycardia)
Closed-loop obstruction on CT
Complete obstruction with no flatus or faeces
Volvulus with haemodynamic compromise
content: Small bowel obstruction (SBO) occurs when the normal passage of intestinal contents is impeded, most commonly due to adhesions from prior abdominal surgery (accounting for 60–70% of cases), followed by external hernias (inguinal, femoral, umbilical), neoplasms, Crohn's disease-related strictures, intussusception, and volvulus. The clinical presentation includes colicky central abdominal pain, vomiting (bilious initially, becoming faeculent in distal obstruction), abdominal distension, and absolute constipation with failure to pass flatus. High-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds with intermittent silence on auscultation suggest mechanical obstruction. Erect abdominal X-ray demonstrates dilated small bowel loops (>3 cm diameter) with air-fluid levels and absence of colonic gas. CT abdomen and pelvis with oral and IV contrast is the gold standard investigation, accurately identifying the site, level, and cause of obstruction, as well as detecting complications such as ischaemia, closed-loop obstruction, and free gas. Signs of strangulated bowel — peritonism, fever, elevated lactate, pneumatosis intestinalis or portal gas on CT — mandate emergency surgical intervention. Adhesional SBO without features of strangulation may be managed conservatively with nasogastric decompression, IV fluid resuscitation, and electrolyte correction for 24–48 hours. Gastrografin swallow (water-soluble contrast) has both diagnostic and therapeutic benefit in adhesional SBO: failure of contrast to reach the colon within 24 hours predicts the need for surgery. Surgical exploration via laparotomy or laparoscopy is indicated for strangulation, closed-loop obstruction, failure of conservative management, or virgin abdomen (no prior surgery) where hernia is suspected. All patients require careful monitoring of urine output, lactate, electrolytes, and clinical status during conservative trial, with low threshold for escalation to theatre.

title: Peptic Ulcer Disease and Helicobacter pylori: Diagnosis and Eradication Therapy
red_flags: Haematemesis or melaena (upper GI bleed)
Sudden severe epigastric pain (perforation)
Iron deficiency anaemia with dyspepsia in patients >55
Weight loss with dyspepsia and vomiting
content: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) results from disruption of the normal mucosal protective mechanisms in the stomach or proximal duodenum, leading to mucosal erosion and ulceration. The two principal aetiologies are Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection — responsible for approximately 80% of duodenal ulcers and 70% of gastric ulcers — and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or aspirin use. H. pylori is a Gram-negative bacterium colonising the gastric mucosa of approximately 50% of the world's population, acquired predominantly in childhood via the faecal-oral route, with higher prevalence in developing countries and lower socioeconomic settings. Symptoms of uncomplicated PUD include epigastric pain or burning, often related to meals — classically worse with eating in gastric ulcers and relieved by eating in duodenal ulcers — nausea, early satiety, and belching. Complications include upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage (haematemesis, melaena), gastric outlet obstruction (vomiting of undigested food), and perforation (sudden severe epigastric pain, board-like rigidity, generalised peritonism, and free air on erect chest X-ray). Diagnosis is established by upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, allowing direct visualisation, biopsy of gastric ulcers for histological exclusion of malignancy, and rapid urease testing for H. pylori. Non-invasive testing for H. pylori includes the carbon-13 urea breath test (most accurate non-invasive test), stool antigen test, and serology (unreliable for distinguishing active from past infection). First-line H. pylori eradication therapy uses a seven-day proton pump inhibitor (PPI)-based triple or quadruple regimen guided by local resistance patterns. Standard triple therapy: PPI twice daily + clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily + amoxicillin 1 g twice daily. Bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole) is preferred in areas with high clarithromycin resistance. Test-of-cure following eradication is recommended using urea breath test or stool antigen at four or more weeks after completing therapy.

title: Ulcerative Colitis: Diagnosis, Disease Activity Assessment and Management
red_flags: Acute severe colitis (Truelove and Witts criteria)
Toxic megacolon on X-ray
Profuse rectal bleeding with haemodynamic compromise
Perforation with peritonitis
content: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic, relapsing-remitting inflammatory bowel disease characterised by diffuse mucosal inflammation confined to the colon, extending proximally from the rectum in a continuous pattern. It affects approximately 160 per 100,000 people in Northern Europe and North America and typically presents in young adults aged 15–35 years, though a second incidence peak occurs in the sixth decade. The hallmark symptom is bloody diarrhoea with mucus, often accompanied by urgency, tenesmus, and crampy lower abdominal pain. Disease extent is classified as proctitis (confined to the rectum), left-sided colitis (extending to the splenic flexure), or extensive/pancolitis (proximal to the splenic flexure). Systemic features including fatigue, weight loss, anaemia, and extra-intestinal manifestations — primary sclerosing cholangitis, anterior uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, and peripheral arthropathy — may accompany intestinal disease. Disease activity is assessed by the Simple Clinical Colitis Activity Index (SCCAI) or Mayo Score. Acute severe UC is defined by the Truelove and Witts criteria: more than six stools per day with blood, plus any one of fever >37.8°C, heart rate >90 bpm, haemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, or ESR >30 mm/hr. Acute severe UC requires hospitalisation, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily, correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances, thromboprophylaxis, and urgent gastroenterology review. Rescue therapy with IV cyclosporin or infliximab should be instituted if there is failure to respond within three days. Colectomy is indicated for failure of medical rescue therapy, toxic megacolon, perforation, or life-threatening haemorrhage. Maintenance therapy for mild-to-moderate UC includes 5-aminosalicylate preparations (mesalazine oral and topical); for moderate-to-severe disease or steroid-dependent cases, immunomodulators (thiopurines, methotrexate) or biologics (anti-TNF agents, vedolizumab, ustekinumab) are used. All UC patients with pancolitis of 10 or more years' duration require colonoscopic surveillance for colorectal cancer.

title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome: Diagnosis, Stratification and Evidence-Based Management
red_flags: Rectal bleeding with IBS-type symptoms
Unexplained weight loss with bowel symptoms
New IBS-type symptoms in patients over 50
Nocturnal diarrhoea or persistent elevated faecal calprotectin
content: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a chronic, functional gastrointestinal disorder characterised by recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and associated with a change in stool frequency or form, occurring at least once per week for the past three months, with symptom onset at least six months before diagnosis. It is classified by the Rome IV criteria into IBS with predominant constipation (IBS-C), IBS with predominant diarrhoea (IBS-D), IBS with mixed bowel habits (IBS-M), and IBS unclassified (IBS-U). IBS is estimated to affect 10–15% of the global population and is the most common reason for gastroenterology referral. The pathophysiology involves altered gut-brain axis signalling, intestinal dysmotility, visceral hypersensitivity, low-grade mucosal inflammation, altered microbiome composition, and psychosocial factors. Diagnosis is clinical in patients under 50 without alarm features; extensive investigation is not required unless alarm features are present: unexplained weight loss, rectal bleeding, iron deficiency anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, persistent diarrhoea with elevated faecal calprotectin, family history of IBD or colorectal cancer, or new symptom onset after age 50. Basic investigations should include FBC, ESR, CRP, coeliac serology (tTG IgA), and thyroid function. Faecal calprotectin is a useful non-invasive marker to differentiate IBS from IBD: a level below 50 μg/g has a high negative predictive value for significant mucosal inflammation. Management is stepwise and tailored to the dominant symptom pattern. Dietary modifications — low-FODMAP diet (reducing fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols) under dietitian supervision — produce symptom improvement in up to 70% of patients. Psychological therapies (CBT, gut-directed hypnotherapy) have robust evidence. Pharmacotherapy includes antispasmodics (mebeverine, hyoscine), laxatives and linaclotide for IBS-C, loperamide or eluxadoline for IBS-D, and low-dose tricyclic antidepressants for pain-predominant symptoms.

title: Chronic Pancreatitis: Diagnosis, Pain Management and Complications
red_flags: Acute-on-chronic pancreatitis with organ failure
New pancreatic mass in chronic pancreatitis (carcinoma)
Severe weight loss with exocrine insufficiency
Gastric varices from splenic vein thrombosis
content: Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disorder characterised by irreversible structural changes in the pancreatic parenchyma — fibrosis, ductal distortion, and calcifications — resulting in permanent impairment of both exocrine (digestive enzyme) and endocrine (insulin) function. The most common aetiology in the United Kingdom is chronic alcohol excess (60–70%), followed by idiopathic disease, hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR mutations), autoimmune pancreatitis (IgG4-related), and obstructive causes. The clinical triad of abdominal pain, steatorrhoea, and diabetes mellitus characterises advanced disease, though presentation varies. Abdominal pain — epigastric, often radiating to the back, partially relieved by leaning forward — is the dominant symptom and is frequently severe and debilitating. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) manifests as malabsorption with steatorrhoea (pale, greasy, difficult-to-flush stools), weight loss, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (A, D, E, K). Endocrine failure (pancreatogenic or type 3c diabetes) is distinct from type 2 diabetes in its unpredictability, hypoglycaemia risk, and absence of insulin resistance. Diagnosis is established by CT and/or MRI/MRCP demonstrating parenchymal calcifications, ductal changes (dilation, strictures, filling defects), and pancreatic atrophy. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is the most sensitive modality for early-stage disease. Faecal elastase-1 is the standard non-invasive test for EPI. Management includes complete alcohol and tobacco cessation (smoking independently worsens disease progression), pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) with high-lipase preparations for EPI, optimisation of diabetes, fat-soluble vitamin supplementation, and pain management (paracetamol, NSAIDs, neuropathic agents, opioids as a last resort). Endoscopic or surgical drainage procedures — endoscopic retrograde pancreatography (ERCP) with stone extraction and ductal stenting, or surgical lateral pancreaticojejunostomy — are indicated for ductal hypertension-related pain.

title: Colorectal Cancer Symptoms: Recognition, Urgent Referral and Surveillance
red_flags: Rectal bleeding with change in bowel habit in patients over 40
Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia
Abdominal mass on examination
Emergency presentation with large bowel obstruction
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الجهاز الهضمي وجراحة القولون والمستقيم
content: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the fourth most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the United Kingdom, with approximately 42,000 new cases diagnosed annually. Early detection through symptom recognition and population-based screening programmes significantly improves survival: five-year survival rates exceed 90% for stage I disease but fall below 10% for metastatic stage IV. Symptoms that should trigger urgent two-week-wait (2WW) referral for colorectal assessment include rectal bleeding with change in bowel habit (looser stools or increased frequency) in patients aged 40 and above, unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in adults, and palpable abdominal or rectal mass. Symptoms in patients aged 50 and above that meet lower-threshold referral criteria include rectal bleeding without anal symptoms, change in bowel habit without rectal bleeding lasting more than six weeks, and unexplained weight loss with abdominal symptoms. Left-sided CRC classically presents with alternating constipation and diarrhoea, rectal bleeding, and tenesmus. Right-sided CRC more commonly produces iron deficiency anaemia, right iliac fossa mass, and occult blood loss with less obvious alteration in bowel habit. Emergency presentations include large bowel obstruction, perforation, and significant haemorrhage. CT colonoscopy (virtual colonoscopy) or flexible colonoscopy is the diagnostic gold standard, allowing direct visualisation, biopsy, and polyp removal. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis is essential for staging. The NHS bowel cancer screening programme (BCSP) offers home faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) to adults aged 50–74 every two years, with colonoscopy for positive tests. Lynch syndrome — hereditary mismatch repair deficiency — accounts for 3–5% of CRC and should be considered in patients with early-onset CRC, multiple synchronous cancers, or family history meeting Amsterdam criteria; referral for genetic counselling and testing is appropriate.

title: Alcoholic Liver Disease: Spectrum, Acute Presentation and Management
red_flags: Acute alcoholic hepatitis with Maddrey discriminant function >32
Hepatorenal syndrome (rising creatinine with cirrhosis)
Variceal haemorrhage with cirrhosis
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
content: Alcohol-related liver disease (ARLD) encompasses a spectrum of hepatic injury — hepatic steatosis (fatty liver), alcoholic hepatitis, alcoholic cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma — caused by chronic excessive alcohol consumption. It is the most common cause of liver-related mortality in the United Kingdom. Fatty liver is the earliest and most prevalent stage, occurring in up to 90% of heavy drinkers; it is typically asymptomatic and potentially reversible with alcohol abstinence. Alcoholic steatohepatitis is characterised by inflammation and hepatocyte ballooning, progressing in some patients to fibrosis and cirrhosis. Alcoholic hepatitis is an acute clinical syndrome superimposed on chronic liver injury, presenting with jaundice, right upper quadrant pain or tenderness, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers in the context of ongoing or recent heavy alcohol use. The Maddrey discriminant function (DF = 4.6 × [PT − control PT] + serum bilirubin in μmol/L ÷ 17) stratifies severity: DF ≥32 indicates severe alcoholic hepatitis with 30-day mortality exceeding 30%, warranting consideration of corticosteroid therapy (prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days) after exclusion of active infection. The Lille score at day 7 assesses steroid response and guides continuation or discontinuation. Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) — a potentially reversible form of acute kidney injury in cirrhotic patients triggered by bacterial infection, haemorrhage, or large-volume paracentesis without adequate albumin replacement — is managed with terlipressin and albumin infusion. Oesophageal varices (grade II–III) complicating portal hypertension require urgent endoscopic variceal band ligation or injection sclerotherapy with IV terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone). Long-term management centres on complete alcohol abstinence — the single most effective intervention — alongside nutritional support (enteral or parenteral in severe malnutrition), thiamine supplementation, and referral to specialist addiction services.

title: Viral Hepatitis B and C: Global Diagnosis, Treatment Eligibility and Elimination Targets
red_flags: Acute liver failure with hepatitis B reactivation
Hepatocellular carcinoma complicating chronic hepatitis
Jaundice with coagulopathy in acute hepatitis
Hepatic decompensation in chronic hepatitis
content: Viral hepatitis B (HBV) and C (HCV) represent global public health emergencies: approximately 296 million people live with chronic HBV infection and 58 million with chronic HCV worldwide, contributing to over 1.1 million deaths annually from cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The WHO 2030 viral hepatitis elimination targets aim to reduce new infections by 90% and mortality by 65%. Hepatitis B is transmitted via parenteral exposure to infected blood, sexual contact, and mother-to-child perinatal transmission, the latter responsible for the majority of chronic HBV infections in high-prevalence regions. Universal neonatal vaccination is the most effective prevention strategy. Chronic HBV is defined as persistence of HBsAg for more than six months; it encompasses immune-tolerant, immune-active (HBeAg-positive and negative), and inactive carrier phases. Indications for antiviral treatment include HBV DNA above 2,000 IU/mL with elevated ALT or significant hepatic fibrosis on biopsy or non-invasive assessment (FibroScan, FIB-4). Preferred first-line agents are entecavir or tenofovir (alafenamide or disoproxil fumarate), which achieve viral suppression in >95% of patients and reduce HCC risk. HCV is a rapidly evolving curable infection: pan-genotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens (sofosbuvir-velpatasvir, glecaprevir-pibrentasvir) achieve sustained virological response (SVR, defined as undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment completion) in over 95% of patients, constituting a functional cure. Treatment is recommended for all individuals with chronic HCV regardless of disease stage. All patients with cirrhosis should undergo six-monthly ultrasound surveillance with AFP for HCC detection, and upper endoscopy for variceal screening. HCV testing by third-generation anti-HCV antibody followed by HCV RNA confirmation is recommended for all persons born between 1945–1965, those with a history of injecting drug use, and blood product recipients prior to 1992.

title: Dysentery and Acute Diarrhoeal Diseases: WHO Global Case Management and Prevention
red_flags: Profuse watery diarrhoea with severe dehydration (cholera)
Bloody diarrhoea with high fever in children (HUS risk)
Severe dehydration with altered consciousness
Septicaemia complicating intestinal infection
content: Acute diarrhoeal diseases remain among the leading causes of childhood mortality globally, responsible for approximately 1.7 billion episodes and over 525,000 deaths in children under five annually, the majority in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Dysentery — defined as diarrhoea with blood and mucus in the stool — is caused most commonly by Shigella species (bacterial dysentery), Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery), Campylobacter jejuni, enteroinvasive E. coli, and Salmonella non-typhi. The WHO integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI) framework classifies acute diarrhoea by clinical severity: no dehydration, some dehydration, and severe dehydration. Dehydration assessment includes skin turgor, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill, urine output, and mental state. Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the cornerstone of treatment for mild-to-moderate dehydration. WHO low-osmolarity ORS (245 mOsm/L) reduces stool output and vomiting compared to standard ORS and is the globally recommended formulation. Severe dehydration with shock requires IV Ringer's lactate (100 mL/kg over three hours in children) with close monitoring. Zinc supplementation (20 mg/day for 10–14 days in children over six months) reduces diarrhoea duration, severity, and recurrence. Breastfeeding should be continued throughout illness. Antibiotic therapy is recommended for severe or invasive bacterial infections: azithromycin is preferred for Shigella in areas with ciprofloxacin resistance; metronidazole for amoebic dysentery. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — a triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, and acute kidney injury — complicates infection with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 and requires avoidance of antimotility agents and antibiotics in suspected STEC infection. Cholera — profuse, painless rice-water diarrhoea caused by Vibrio cholerae — demands rapid fluid resuscitation and doxycycline or azithromycin treatment.

title: Oesophageal Disorders: Achalasia, GORD and Barrett's Oesophagus
red_flags: Dysphagia with weight loss (suspected malignancy)
Achalasia with aspiration pneumonia
Barrett's oesophagus with dysplasia (pre-malignant change)
Severe GORD with haematemesis
content: Oesophageal disorders encompass a spectrum of conditions affecting swallowing, motility, mucosal integrity, and structural anatomy of the oesophagus. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) is the most prevalent oesophageal condition, defined by troublesome symptoms or complications resulting from retrograde movement of gastric contents into the oesophagus. Classic symptoms include heartburn and acid regurgitation; atypical presentations include chronic cough, laryngitis, non-cardiac chest pain, and asthma. Diagnosis is clinical in typical cases; upper GI endoscopy is indicated for alarm symptoms (dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, haematemesis, anaemia), failure of empirical PPI therapy, or symptom duration exceeding five years to screen for Barrett's oesophagus. Barrett's oesophagus — metaplastic replacement of squamous oesophageal epithelium with specialised intestinal epithelium — is a premalignant condition caused by chronic acid exposure, with an estimated risk of progression to oesophageal adenocarcinoma of 0.3–0.5% per year; patients require endoscopic surveillance at three-yearly intervals (non-dysplastic) or annually (low-grade dysplasia). High-grade dysplasia warrants endoscopic mucosal resection or radiofrequency ablation. Achalasia — the most common primary oesophageal motility disorder — results from degeneration of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, causing failure of lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) relaxation and absent peristalsis. Presentation includes progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, weight loss, and chest discomfort. Barium swallow demonstrates the classic 'bird-beak' or 'rat-tail' narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction. High-resolution oesophageal manometry is the gold standard, showing absent peristalsis and impaired LOS relaxation with elevated resting pressure. Treatment options include endoscopic pneumatic balloon dilation, per-oral endoscopic myotomy (POEM), or Heller myotomy (with partial fundoplication). Oesophageal carcinoma — squamous cell carcinoma (proximal) and adenocarcinoma (distal) — must be excluded in all patients with progressive dysphagia.

title: Malnutrition and Intestinal Malabsorption: Global Assessment and Management
red_flags: Severe acute malnutrition with oedema (kwashiorkor)
Refeeding syndrome risk in prolonged starvation
Weight loss >10% with diarrhoea (malabsorption)
New severe malabsorption with dermatitis and neuropathy (pellagra/coeliac)
content: Malnutrition and intestinal malabsorption represent interconnected global health challenges affecting both low-income settings — where undernutrition and infectious causes predominate — and high-income countries — where disease-related malnutrition, coeliac disease, and inflammatory bowel disease are more prevalent. Intestinal malabsorption results from defective digestion, impaired mucosal absorption, or lymphatic obstruction, producing fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, protein-calorie malnutrition, and micronutrient deficiencies. Common causes include coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy), lactase deficiency, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, Crohn's disease, tropical sprue, Whipple's disease, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), and post-surgical short bowel syndrome. Coeliac disease affects approximately 1% of the global population and is caused by an immune-mediated response to dietary gluten in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2 or DQ8). It presents with diarrhoea, bloating, weight loss, fatigue, iron deficiency anaemia, and dermatitis herpetiformis. Diagnosis requires positive tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody and duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy (Marsh grade III). Treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet. SIBO — excessive bacterial colonisation of the small intestine — causes malabsorption, bloating, flatulence, and diarrhoea; diagnosis is by glucose or lactulose hydrogen breath testing; treatment with rifaximin or rotating antibiotics. WHO guidelines on severe acute malnutrition (SAM) emphasise the F75/F100 therapeutic milk protocol with structured rehabilitation phases. Refeeding syndrome — hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, and fluid shifts precipitated by rapid nutritional repletion in malnourished patients — requires slow reintroduction of nutrition with careful electrolyte monitoring and supplementation. Nutritional support should be tailored to underlying cause, with dietitian involvement and regular monitoring of anthropometric, biochemical, and functional nutritional parameters.

title: Acute Mesenteric Ischaemia: Recognition, Urgency and Surgical Management
red_flags: Severe diffuse abdominal pain out of proportion to examination findings
Peritonitis with lactic acidosis and elevated WBC
Atrial fibrillation with sudden severe abdominal pain (embolic)
CT showing pneumatosis intestinalis or portal gas
content: Acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI) is a life-threatening vascular emergency caused by inadequate blood supply to the small intestine, resulting in bowel infarction, perforation, and septic shock if not recognised and treated within hours. It carries a mortality rate exceeding 60–80% even with treatment, largely due to delayed diagnosis. The four main subtypes are: arterial embolism (most common, 50%, arising from AF, cardiac mural thrombus, or atherosclerotic plaque), arterial thrombosis (25%, in patients with pre-existing mesenteric atherosclerosis), non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (NOMI, 20%, in low-flow states such as cardiogenic shock, sepsis, or vasoconstricting drugs), and mesenteric venous thrombosis (5–10%, associated with hypercoagulable states). The classic presentation of arterial embolism is the sudden onset of severe, crampy, periumbilical abdominal pain that is dramatically out of proportion to physical findings on examination — a hallmark diagnostic clue. As ischaemia progresses to infarction and transmural necrosis, the abdomen becomes peritonitic, rigid, and silent, with systemic features of sepsis and multiorgan dysfunction. Laboratory findings include markedly elevated lactate, elevated WBC, and metabolic acidosis. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis is the investigation of choice and can identify arterial occlusion, bowel wall thickening, portal venous gas, and pneumatosis intestinalis. Treatment involves immediate resuscitation with IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, anticoagulation, and urgent vascular surgery or interventional radiology consultation. Surgical revascularisation — embolectomy, bypass, or thrombectomy — with second-look laparotomy to assess bowel viability within 24–36 hours is the standard approach for arterial occlusion with peritonitis. Endovascular techniques (catheter-directed thrombolysis, angioplasty) may be used in selected patients without peritonism. Mesenteric venous thrombosis is managed with anticoagulation and treatment of underlying thrombophilia.

title: Nausea, Vomiting and Gastroparesis: Differential Diagnosis and Management
red_flags: Vomiting undigested food hours after meals (gastroparesis)
Severe vomiting with electrolyte derangement and metabolic alkalosis
Protracted vomiting with haematemesis
Hyperemesis with jaundice (Wernicke's risk)
content: Nausea and vomiting are among the most common gastrointestinal complaints, with an extensive differential diagnosis spanning neurological, metabolic, obstructive, and functional causes. Clinicians must systematically exclude life-threatening causes — raised intracranial pressure, myocardial infarction, diabetic ketoacidosis, Addisonian crisis, bowel obstruction, and mesenteric ischaemia — before attributing symptoms to functional or benign aetiology. The character, timing, and content of vomitus are diagnostically informative: projectile vomiting without nausea suggests raised ICP; bilious vomiting indicates an obstruction distal to the ampulla; faeculent vomiting suggests distal small bowel or colonic obstruction; vomiting of undigested food hours after meals is characteristic of gastroparesis. Gastroparesis is a syndrome of delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction, most commonly caused by diabetes mellitus (diabetic autonomic neuropathy), post-surgical vagal damage, or idiopathic aetiology. Diagnosis is confirmed by gastric emptying scintigraphy — the gold standard — demonstrating prolonged retention of radiolabelled food: more than 60% retention at two hours or more than 10% at four hours defines delayed emptying. Management includes dietary modification (small, frequent, low-fat, low-fibre meals), optimisation of glycaemic control in diabetics, and prokinetic therapy. Metoclopramide (dopamine D2 antagonist) is the first-line pharmacological agent but carries a risk of tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use. Domperidone provides peripheral prokinesis with less central side effect risk. Erythromycin (a motilin receptor agonist) can be used short-term for refractory cases. Venting gastrostomy or jejunal feeding tube may be required in severe, nutrition-compromising gastroparesis. Hyperemesis gravidarum — severe vomiting in pregnancy causing dehydration, ketonaemia, and weight loss exceeding 5% — requires hospitalisation, IV hydration, thiamine supplementation, and antiemetic therapy.

title: Crohn's Disease: Diagnosis, Disease Behaviour Classification and Biological Therapy
red_flags: Acute intestinal obstruction due to Crohn's stricture
Fistulising Crohn's with sepsis (intraabdominal abscess)
Perianal sepsis with fever
Crohn's flare with entero-vesical fistula
content: Crohn's disease (CD) is a chronic, transmural, granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease that may affect any segment of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the perianal region, with the terminal ileum and ileocaecal region most commonly involved. The Montreal classification characterises disease by age at diagnosis (A1–A3), location (L1–L4), and behaviour (B1 inflammatory, B2 stricturing, B3 penetrating, with perianal modifier p). Symptoms depend on disease location: ileocaecal CD produces right lower quadrant pain and diarrhoea; colonic CD mimics ulcerative colitis with bloody diarrhoea; upper GI involvement causes dysphagia or epigastric pain; perianal disease presents with painful fissures, fistulae, and abscess formation. Systemic features — weight loss, fatigue, low-grade fever — and extra-intestinal manifestations (peripheral arthropathy, sacroiliitis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, primary sclerosing cholangitis) are common. Diagnosis combines clinical assessment with ileocolonoscopy and biopsy (transmural granulomatous inflammation), small bowel MRI (for small intestinal extent, strictures, and fistulae), and cross-sectional CT imaging for acute complications. Faecal calprotectin is elevated during active mucosal inflammation. CRP and serum albumin reflect systemic inflammatory burden and nutritional status. Remission induction in mild-to-moderate disease may use exclusive enteral nutrition (particularly in paediatric patients) or controlled ileal release budesonide for ileocaecal CD. Moderate-to-severe disease requires anti-TNF agents (infliximab, adalimumab), anti-integrin therapy (vedolizumab), or anti-IL-12/23 (ustekinumab). Combination therapy with immunomodulators (azathioprine, methotrexate) reduces immunogenicity. Surgical resection is indicated for refractory strictures, abscesses unresponsive to antibiotics, fistulae causing significant morbidity, and emergencies. Perianal sepsis requires examination under anaesthesia, seton placement, and long-term medical therapy.
