title: Acute Appendicitis: Scoring Systems, Imaging and Surgical Management
red_flags: Perforation with generalised peritonitis
Septic shock with appendicitis
Mass in RIF (appendiceal abscess or mass)
Appendicitis in pregnancy (atypical location, fetal risk)
content: Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency worldwide, affecting approximately 7–8% of individuals over their lifetime, with peak incidence in the second and third decades. It results from obstruction of the appendiceal lumen — by faecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia, or less commonly tumour — leading to bacterial overgrowth, mucosal ischaemia, transmural inflammation, and eventual perforation if untreated. The classic presentation is periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa (RIF) over 24–48 hours, associated with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. Physical examination reveals localised RIF tenderness, Rovsing's sign (RIF pain on palpation of LIF), psoas sign (pain on passive hip extension in retrocaecal appendicitis), and rebound tenderness. Perforation is suggested by generalised peritonitis, high fever, tachycardia, and markedly elevated WBC. The Alvarado score and Appendicitis Inflammatory Response (AIR) score integrate clinical and laboratory features (migration of pain, anorexia, nausea, RIF tenderness, rebound tenderness, temperature, WBC, CRP) to stratify the probability of appendicitis. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality in children and pregnant women; CT abdomen and pelvis (with contrast) has high sensitivity (>95%) and specificity (>95%) for appendicitis in adults and is preferred when ultrasound is inconclusive. MRI is used in pregnancy to avoid radiation. Management is surgical in most cases: laparoscopic appendicectomy is preferred over open surgery for shorter hospital stay, reduced wound infection, and faster return to normal activities. Non-operative management with antibiotics alone (piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone with metronidazole) is an emerging option for uncomplicated appendicitis in selected patients, with a 30% failure rate requiring surgery within five years. Appendiceal masses or periappendicular abscesses may be managed initially with IV antibiotics and CT-guided drainage, with interval appendicectomy considered after 6–8 weeks. Atypical presentations occur in pregnancy (appendix displaced superiorly by gravid uterus), elderly patients (blunted inflammatory response, higher perforation rate), and immunocompromised individuals.

title: Septic Arthritis: Emergency Diagnosis and Arthrocentesis
red_flags: Hot swollen joint with fever (septic until proven otherwise)
Septic arthritis in immunocompromised patient
Failure to improve within 48 hours of antibiotics
Septic arthritis with adjacent osteomyelitis
content: Septic arthritis is an orthopaedic emergency caused by bacterial infection within a synovial joint, most commonly resulting from haematogenous seeding or direct inoculation following trauma, surgery, or joint aspiration. It carries significant morbidity — including rapid cartilage destruction and permanent joint damage — and mortality if not treated promptly. Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) is the most common causative organism across all age groups. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the most common cause in sexually active young adults and may present with migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, and skin lesions (gonococcal disseminated infection). Streptococcal species, Gram-negative bacilli (in elderly, immunocompromised, or IV drug users), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (in IV drug users) are also implicated. The classic presentation is a single, acutely painful, swollen, warm, and erythematous joint with restricted movement and fever. The knee is the most commonly affected joint, followed by the hip (particularly in infants), shoulder, ankle, and wrist. Any hot swollen joint must be treated as septic arthritis until proven otherwise by joint aspiration. Arthrocentesis (joint aspiration) is mandatory and must not be delayed. Synovial fluid with a white cell count above 50,000 cells/mm³ with more than 75% polymorphonuclear cells is strongly suggestive of infection; Gram stain positivity is diagnostic; culture confirms the organism and guides antibiotic sensitivity. Blood cultures should be taken simultaneously. Plain X-rays are taken to exclude associated fracture or osteomyelitis; MRI with gadolinium is superior for detecting early osteomyelitis, joint effusion, and soft tissue involvement. IV antibiotic therapy should be commenced immediately after aspiration: empirical flucloxacillin 2 g four times daily (or vancomycin if MRSA risk) pending sensitivities. Repeated joint aspiration (by arthrocentesis or arthroscopy) or surgical washout is required for joints that do not respond to antibiotics within 48 hours or for large joint involvement (hip in children). Duration of IV antibiotics is typically two weeks, followed by oral therapy for a total of four to six weeks.

title: Stress Fractures: Recognition, Imaging and Return-to-Activity Guidance
red_flags: Anterior tibial stress fracture (high-risk non-union)
Femoral neck stress fracture (risk of displacement and AVN)
Navicular stress fracture in athlete (high-risk site)
Stress fracture with underlying metabolic bone disease
content: Stress fractures are overuse injuries resulting from repetitive mechanical loading on bone that exceeds the bone's ability to remodel and repair, occurring without a single traumatic event. They are classified as fatigue fractures (normal bone subjected to abnormal loading, common in athletes and military recruits) or insufficiency fractures (normal loading on osteoporotic or metabolically compromised bone). They are most prevalent in athletes engaged in high-impact activities — running, gymnastics, basketball, and military training — and account for 1–10% of all sports injuries. Common sites include the tibia (most common), metatarsals (second through fourth), fibula, femoral shaft, femoral neck, navicular, calcaneus, and sacrum. High-risk sites — where non-union, displacement, and avascular necrosis are significant risks — include the femoral neck (anterior cortex), anterior tibial cortex ('dreaded black line'), navicular, proximal fifth metatarsal (Jones fracture zone), and medial malleolus. The clinical presentation is insidious, localised bony pain aggravated by activity and relieved by rest, with point tenderness on palpation of the affected bone. Plain X-rays are frequently negative in the first 2–3 weeks; a periosteal reaction or cortical breach may develop later. MRI is the gold standard for diagnosis, demonstrating periosteal oedema and bone marrow signal change on T2-weighted sequences, and accurately identifies high-risk fracture patterns. Nuclear bone scan offers high sensitivity. CT is useful for characterising cortical involvement. The female athlete triad — low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, and low bone mineral density — is a significant risk factor for stress fractures in female athletes and should be systematically evaluated. Treatment for low-risk fractures involves relative rest, activity modification, and graduated return to sport over 4–8 weeks. High-risk fractures require non-weight-bearing immobilisation, orthopaedic referral, and may necessitate surgical fixation to prevent catastrophic displacement.

title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Diagnosis, Non-surgical Management and Surgical Referral
red_flags: Acute carpal tunnel following wrist fracture or haematoma
Complete thenar muscle wasting (irreversible nerve damage)
Bilateral carpal tunnel with systemic disease (amyloid, acromegaly)
Rapidly progressive symptoms with severe electrophysiological changes
content: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is the most common peripheral entrapment neuropathy, caused by compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel — an anatomically rigid compartment bounded by the carpal bones dorsally and the flexor retinaculum volarly. It has a population prevalence of 3–6% and predominantly affects women aged 40–60. Compression results in median nerve dysfunction manifesting as paraesthesiae (tingling, numbness, burning), pain in the thumb, index, middle, and radial aspect of the ring finger, and in advanced cases, weakness and wasting of the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis). Symptoms are classically worse at night and may wake patients from sleep; activities requiring sustained wrist flexion or extension (driving, holding a phone, reading) exacerbate symptoms. Phalen's manoeuvre (wrist held in maximal flexion for 60 seconds) and Tinel's sign (percussion over the carpal tunnel at the wrist) are provocative clinical tests with moderate sensitivity and specificity. Risk factors include obesity, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, acromegaly, amyloidosis, and wrist trauma. Nerve conduction studies (NCS) are the gold standard for diagnosis, demonstrating prolonged median nerve sensory and motor distal latencies and reduced amplitudes, and also quantify severity to guide management. Ultrasound of the median nerve at the wrist, measuring cross-sectional area (CTA >10 mm² suggesting CTS), is an emerging and increasingly used diagnostic tool. Conservative management includes nocturnal wrist splinting in a neutral position, activity modification, and corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel (useful for diagnosis confirmation and short-to-medium term relief). Surgical carpal tunnel decompression (open or endoscopic release of the flexor retinaculum) is recommended for moderate-to-severe CTS, failure of conservative therapy, thenar wasting, and electrophysiologically severe disease. Surgical outcomes are excellent, with symptom resolution in 80–90% of patients.

title: Bursitis: Diagnosis, Site-Specific Management and Red Flag Identification
red_flags: Septic bursitis (fever with fluctuant hot bursa)
Olecranon or prepatellar bursitis following trauma with skin breach
Refractory bursitis with systemic disease (gout, RA)
Rapidly enlarging bursa with malignancy concern
content: Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa — a small fluid-filled sac located at sites of friction between tendons, muscles, and bony prominences — resulting in localised pain, swelling, warmth, and restricted movement. Common anatomical sites include the subacromial bursa (shoulder), olecranon bursa (elbow), prepatellar bursa (knee, associated with prolonged kneeling — 'housemaid's knee'), infrapatellar bursa, trochanteric bursa (hip, causing greater trochanteric pain syndrome), and retrocalcaneal bursa (Achilles). Bursitis may be acute or chronic and arises from repetitive mechanical friction, direct trauma, or inflammatory systemic conditions (rheumatoid arthritis, gout, pseudogout, psoriatic arthritis). Septic bursitis — caused by bacterial infection, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus following skin trauma or abrasion — must be excluded in all acute presentations with fever, marked erythema, and systemic signs. Bursal aspiration is diagnostic and therapeutic: synovial fluid with white cell count above 20,000/mm³ with polymorphonuclear predominance, positive Gram stain, or culture is diagnostic of septic bursitis. Crystal analysis identifies urate (gout) or calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout). Non-septic bursitis is managed conservatively with RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation), NSAIDs, and activity modification. Corticosteroid injection into the bursa provides effective short-to-medium term relief for subacromial and trochanteric bursitis when conservative measures fail. Septic bursitis requires IV antibiotics (flucloxacillin or vancomycin), repeated aspiration, and surgical bursectomy for refractory or recurrent infection. Ultrasound is useful for confirming the presence and extent of bursitis, guiding aspiration, and excluding associated tendon tears. Chronic refractory bursitis unresponsive to conservative and injection therapy may require surgical excision of the bursa.

title: Fibromyalgia Syndrome: Diagnosis, Multi-modal Treatment and Specialist Referral
red_flags: New widespread pain with systemic features (exclude malignancy or inflammatory disease)
Fibromyalgia with objective neurological signs (not typical)
Severe cognitive impairment ('fibro fog') with new onset
Associated unrefreshing sleep with mood disorder and self-harm risk
content: Fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS) is a chronic, widespread musculoskeletal pain disorder characterised by diffuse pain affecting multiple body regions, fatigue, non-restorative sleep, and cognitive difficulties ('fibro fog'). It affects approximately 2–8% of the population globally, with a strong female predominance (female-to-male ratio of 7:1), and is a significant cause of disability and reduced quality of life. The 2016 revised fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria (American College of Rheumatology) require a widespread pain index (WPI) of 7 or above plus symptom severity scale score of 5 or above, or WPI of 4–6 plus symptom severity scale of 9 or above, with symptoms present at similar level for at least three months, and no other disorder that would otherwise explain the pain. Fibromyalgia does not cause tissue inflammation, joint damage, or abnormal routine laboratory findings; its absence in blood tests and imaging is confirmatory. Clinicians must exclude inflammatory arthritis (elevated CRP, ESR, anti-CCP, RF), hypothyroidism, polymyalgia rheumatica, systemic lupus, and malignancy in patients presenting with widespread pain. The pathophysiology of fibromyalgia involves central sensitisation — amplified pain processing in the central nervous system — with abnormal descending pain inhibition, neuroinflammation, and altered sleep architecture. Management is multimodal and evidence-based: aerobic exercise (low-impact — swimming, walking, cycling) is the most effective single intervention for long-term pain and function improvement. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) addresses maladaptive pain cognitions and catastrophising. Pharmacological options include low-dose amitriptyline (10–75 mg nocte) for sleep disturbance and pain, duloxetine (30–60 mg daily) for pain and mood, and pregabalin or gabapentin for neuropathic-type pain. Opioids are not recommended. Patient education regarding the nature of central sensitisation is essential. Multidisciplinary pain management programmes produce superior outcomes compared to unimodal therapy.

title: Osteoporosis in Women: Fracture Risk Assessment, Prevention and Treatment
red_flags: Vertebral fracture with spinal cord compression
Multiple spontaneous low-trauma vertebral fractures
Osteoporosis with hypercalcaemia (secondary cause)
Unexplained bone loss in young woman (<50 years)
content: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disorder characterised by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, resulting in increased bone fragility and susceptibility to fracture, particularly at the hip, spine, and distal forearm. It affects approximately 200 million women worldwide and is a leading cause of disability and mortality in postmenopausal women and older adults. Bone mineral density (BMD) is measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of the lumbar spine and proximal femur; a T-score of -2.5 or below defines osteoporosis; between -1.0 and -2.5 defines osteopenia. The FRAX tool (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool, WHO) calculates the ten-year probability of major osteoporotic fracture and hip fracture based on clinical risk factors — age, sex, BMI, prior fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, glucocorticoid use, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis causes, and alcohol consumption — with or without BMD. All postmenopausal women with FRAX major fracture probability above the intervention threshold (age-dependent), or T-score ≤-2.5, or prior fragility fracture, should be offered treatment. Secondary causes of osteoporosis that must be excluded include corticosteroid excess, hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, coeliac disease, vitamin D deficiency, chronic kidney disease, and malabsorption syndromes. First-line treatment includes calcium (1,000–1,200 mg/day dietary) and vitamin D (800–1,000 IU/day) supplementation alongside oral bisphosphonates — alendronate (70 mg weekly) or risedronate — which reduce vertebral fracture risk by 40–70% and hip fracture risk by 40–50%. For patients intolerant of or unresponsive to oral bisphosphonates, alternatives include zoledronic acid (5 mg IV annually), denosumab (60 mg SC six-monthly), or for high-risk patients, anabolic therapy with teriparatide or romosozumab. All patients should receive fall prevention counselling, home hazard assessment, and referral for balance training.

title: Metastatic Bone Disease and Cancer-Related Spinal Pain: Recognition and Emergency Referral
red_flags: Progressive back pain with known malignancy (spinal metastases)
Bilateral leg weakness with bladder/bowel dysfunction (MSCC)
Night pain unrelieved by rest with elevated inflammatory markers
New vertebral fracture with no adequate trauma history in cancer patient

content: Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) is an oncological emergency defined as compression of the dural sac and its contents — the spinal cord or cauda equina — by extradural metastatic tumour, most commonly from primary cancers of the breast, prostate, lung, kidney, and thyroid, as well as multiple myeloma and lymphoma. Vertebral metastases occur in approximately 40% of cancer patients, most frequently in the thoracic spine (70%), followed by lumbar (20%) and cervical (10%) regions. Early recognition is critical: once complete paralysis is established, recovery of function is rare regardless of treatment. The presenting symptom in 90% of cases is back pain — typically progressive, constant, worse on lying flat, and not relieved by rest — often preceding neurological symptoms by weeks to months. New or worsening back pain in a patient with known or suspected malignancy must be treated as MSCC until proven otherwise. Neurological symptoms and signs include leg weakness (may be asymmetric), sensory loss with or without a dermatomal level, and sphincter dysfunction (urinary retention, constipation, incontinence). Any patient with known cancer and new back pain, or any patient with unexplained back pain and bilateral leg symptoms, should undergo urgent MRI whole spine within 24 hours. Dexamethasone 16 mg IV or oral should be administered immediately upon suspicion of MSCC to reduce cord oedema. Emergency referral to a spinal surgery or oncology team capable of providing definitive treatment (surgical decompression and/or radiotherapy) within 24 hours is mandated. Surgical decompression with posterior stabilisation followed by radiotherapy improves ambulatory outcomes compared to radiotherapy alone in patients with solid tumour MSCC and reasonable prognosis. Radiotherapy alone is appropriate for radiosensitive tumours (lymphoma, myeloma, seminoma), multilevel disease, or patients unfit for surgery. Palliative care input is essential from initial diagnosis.

title: Rotator Cuff Disorders and Shoulder Pain: Assessment and Referral Pathway
red_flags: Shoulder pain with axillary lymphadenopathy (Pancoast or malignancy)
Severe acute pain with complete loss of abduction (complete tear)
Shoulder pain with fever (septic arthritis or osteomyelitis)
Bilateral painful shoulders with constitutional symptoms (inflammatory arthropathy)
content: Shoulder pain is one of the most common musculoskeletal complaints in primary care, with an annual prevalence of 14–21% in the adult population. The rotator cuff — comprising supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis tendons — provides dynamic shoulder stability and facilitates the complex motion arc of the glenohumeral joint. Rotator cuff disorders encompass a spectrum from tendinopathy and calcific deposits to partial and full-thickness tears. Subacromial impingement syndrome — now reclassified within the broader category of subacromial pain syndrome (SAPS) — results from mechanical compression of the supraspinatus tendon between the acromion and humeral head during shoulder elevation, producing arc pain (between 60–120 degrees of abduction). Complete rotator cuff tears present with severe limitation of active shoulder movement (inability to initiate abduction), weakness (particularly external rotation and abduction), and chronic pain. The painful arc test, Hawkins-Kennedy test, Neer's sign, Jobe's test (empty can), and lag signs are clinical tests used to assess impingement and rotator cuff integrity. MRI arthrogram is the gold standard investigation for characterising rotator cuff tears, assessing muscle atrophy, and planning surgical management. Ultrasound is highly operator-dependent but provides dynamic assessment and is widely available. Differential diagnoses include glenohumeral osteoarthritis, adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder), acromioclavicular joint pathology, biceps tendinopathy, cervical radiculopathy, and referred pain from cardiac or diaphragmatic pathology (must be excluded in left shoulder pain). Management includes physiotherapy targeting rotator cuff strengthening and scapular control, subacromial corticosteroid injection for symptom relief, and surgical repair (arthroscopic or open) for full-thickness tears in active patients or those failing conservative therapy for three to six months. Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is managed with physiotherapy, corticosteroid injection, and hydrodilatation.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis: Global Management Standards and Treat-to-Target Strategy
red_flags: Acute monoarthritis in RA patient (septic arthritis)
Cervical myelopathy from C1-C2 instability in longstanding RA
RA with acute vasculitis (digital ischaemia)
Interstitial lung disease exacerbation in RA
content: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic autoimmune disease characterised by symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, joint destruction, and significant extra-articular manifestations. With a global prevalence of 0.5–1%, it disproportionately affects women (3:1 female-to-male ratio) and peak onset occurs between 40 and 60 years. The underlying pathophysiology involves autoimmune dysregulation — driven by anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA/anti-CCP) and rheumatoid factor (RF) — resulting in synovial hyperplasia (pannus formation), cartilage erosion, and subchondral bone destruction. The American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) 2010 classification criteria score patients on joint involvement, serology, acute phase reactants, and symptom duration to define early RA. Early diagnosis and prompt initiation of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) is essential: the 'window of opportunity' — treating within the first three to twelve months of symptom onset — significantly improves long-term outcomes by preventing irreversible joint damage. The treat-to-target (T2T) strategy mandates regular disease activity monitoring using validated composite scores (DAS28-CRP, CDAI, SDAI) and therapy escalation until remission or low disease activity is achieved. First-line DMARD therapy is methotrexate (starting 10–15 mg weekly, escalating to 25 mg), supplemented with folic acid (5 mg weekly). Hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are added in combination if response is inadequate. Biological DMARDs — anti-TNF agents (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab), abatacept, rituximab, tocilizumab, and sarilumab — are indicated when response to conventional DMARDs is inadequate. Targeted synthetic DMARDs (JAK inhibitors: tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib) represent an effective oral alternative. Extra-articular manifestations requiring specific monitoring include interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, vasculitis, cervical spine instability, and Sjögren's overlap.

title: Osteoarthritis: Global Burden, Non-pharmacological Interventions and Surgical Thresholds
red_flags: Acute locked knee with internal derangement (cruciate or meniscal tear)
Acute monoarthritis with systemic features (septic arthritis or gout)
Rapidly progressive OA in young patient (secondary cause)
Joint pain with constitutional symptoms (malignancy or inflammatory disease)
content: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most prevalent joint disease globally, affecting over 500 million people and representing the leading cause of musculoskeletal disability in older adults. It is a whole-organ disease characterised by progressive cartilage degradation, subchondral bone remodelling, osteophyte formation, synovial inflammation, and periarticular tissue changes. The knee, hip, and hand joints are most commonly affected. The WHO global action plan for musculoskeletal health emphasises that OA is not an inevitable consequence of ageing but is modifiable through targeted lifestyle interventions and appropriate medical management. Clinical diagnosis is based on symptoms (use-related joint pain, morning stiffness <30 minutes, crepitus, bony joint enlargement, restricted range of motion) and typical radiographic features (joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and cyst formation) in the appropriate clinical context. MRI provides superior characterisation of cartilage, meniscal, and bone marrow pathology but is not routinely required for diagnosis. Non-pharmacological interventions — which are the cornerstone of OA management — include therapeutic exercise (aerobic, strengthening, and aquatic exercise), weight reduction in overweight patients (each kilogram of weight loss reduces knee load by four kilograms per step), physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and appropriate footwear and orthotic devices. Patient education regarding self-management, activity pacing, and analgesia is essential. Pharmacological options include topical NSAIDs (preferred for hand and knee OA to reduce systemic side effects), oral NSAIDs with gastroprotection, paracetamol (limited evidence), and intra-articular corticosteroid injections for acute flares. Opioids should be avoided. Surgical referral — total joint arthroplasty — is appropriate when pain is severe, functional limitation is significant, quality of life is impaired, and adequate non-surgical management has been trialled, typically for a minimum of three to six months.

title: Low Back Pain: Global Burden, Evidence-Based Management and Avoidance of Overinvestigation
red_flags: Cauda equina syndrome (bilateral leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, sphincter dysfunction)

Severe night pain in patient over 50 with weight loss (malignancy)
Back pain with bilateral lower limb spasticity (cord compression)
content: Low back pain (LBP) is the leading cause of years lived with disability globally, affecting over 619 million people and representing an enormous economic burden through lost productivity, healthcare utilisation, and disability-related costs. The WHO global action plan on physical activity and musculoskeletal health acknowledges LBP as a priority non-communicable disease requiring population-level and individual-level intervention. Clinically, LBP is classified into: specific (caused by a recognisable pathology — fracture, infection, malignancy, inflammatory spondyloarthropathy, nerve root compression — representing fewer than 5% of cases) and non-specific (no identifiable anatomical cause, 95% of cases). The clinical priority is systematic identification of 'red flags' warranting urgent investigation and specialist referral: cauda equina syndrome (bilateral leg weakness, bilateral radiculopathy, perianal saddle-pattern anaesthesia, urinary retention — an orthopaedic emergency requiring MRI and surgical decompression within 48 hours), suspected malignancy (nocturnal pain, unexplained weight loss, prior cancer history, age over 50, failure to improve), suspected infection (fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression, recent urinary or spinal procedure), and inflammatory spondyloarthropathy (onset under 40, morning stiffness lasting over one hour, alternating buttock pain, improvement with exercise, elevated HLA-B27). For non-specific LBP, clinical guidelines globally converge on a recommendation against routine imaging (plain X-ray, MRI) in the absence of red flags, as incidental findings increase unnecessary interventions. First-line management includes reassurance and education that most LBP improves within four to six weeks, encouragement of physical activity, supervised exercise therapy (strengthening, stretching, aerobic), and consideration of psychological support (CBT) for patients with high distress, catastrophising, or chronicity risk factors (yellow flags). Topical or oral NSAIDs provide modest analgesic benefit for acute LBP. Spinal surgery should be considered only for clearly identified structural pathology correlating with symptoms.

title: Gout and Crystal Arthropathy: Acute Management and Long-Term Urate Lowering
red_flags: Acute gout with septic arthritis (must exclude)
Tophi causing joint destruction or nerve compression
Urate nephropathy with renal failure
Severe refractory tophaceous gout unresponsive to standard ULT
content: Gout is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis worldwide, caused by monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition in joints and soft tissues resulting from sustained hyperuricaemia (serum urate above 6.8 mg/dL or 408 µmol/L). The prevalence of gout is rising globally in parallel with obesity, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and increased consumption of purine-rich foods and fructose-sweetened beverages. The classic presentation of acute gout is a sudden, exquisitely painful, swollen, erythematous, and warm joint — the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) in 50% of initial attacks — typically reaching maximum intensity within 12–24 hours. Other sites include the ankle, knee, wrist, and small joints of the hand. The differential diagnosis of acute monoarthritis includes septic arthritis (which must be excluded by synovial fluid aspiration and culture), pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis, particularly in elderly patients and large joints), reactive arthritis, and trauma. Joint aspiration demonstrating negatively birefringent, needle-shaped MSU crystals under polarised light microscopy is diagnostic. Serum urate may paradoxically be normal during acute attacks. Acute gout is managed with NSAIDs (naproxen, indomethacin), colchicine (0.5 mg two to three times daily for five days), or corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or intraarticular injection) when NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated. Prophylactic colchicine or low-dose NSAID should be continued for the first three to six months after initiating urate-lowering therapy (ULT) to prevent mobilisation flares. ULT is indicated for patients with two or more attacks per year, tophi, urate nephropathy, or renal calculi. Allopurinol (starting 100 mg daily, titrated to target serum urate below 6 mg/dL) is first-line ULT; febuxostat is an alternative. Pegloticase (IV recombinant uricase) is reserved for severe refractory tophaceous gout. Dietary modification — reduced purine intake, alcohol avoidance, increased hydration, and weight loss — and review of medications contributing to hyperuricaemia (thiazide diuretics, low-dose aspirin, cyclosporin) are essential.

title: Ankylosing Spondylitis and Axial Spondyloarthropathy: Diagnosis and Biological Therapy
red_flags: Spinal fracture in ankylosing spondylitis (high-risk — may be unstable)
Acute anterior uveitis with spondylitis
Cauda equina syndrome (arachnoiditis in longstanding AS)

content: Axial spondyloarthropathy (axSpA) is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease primarily affecting the sacroiliac joints and spine, encompassing radiographic axSpA — ankylosing spondylitis (AS), defined by definitive sacroiliitis on plain X-ray — and non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA), where structural changes are absent or detectable only by MRI. AS is the prototypic form, characterised by progressive spinal fusion (ankylosis), chronic inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, peripheral arthritis, and extra-musculoskeletal manifestations. The classic presentation is chronic low back pain and stiffness with onset before age 45, persisting for more than three months, with morning stiffness lasting over one hour that improves with exercise but not rest, and alternating buttock pain from sacroiliac joint involvement. HLA-B27 is present in 90–95% of AS patients of European ancestry (but only 50–60% of Afro-Caribbean patients) and aids diagnosis but is neither necessary nor sufficient. MRI of the sacroiliac joints is the most sensitive method for detecting early inflammatory changes (bone marrow oedema, Romanus lesions) before structural damage on X-ray. The Assessment of SpondyloArthritis International Society (ASAS) criteria classify patients with either sacroiliac joint imaging abnormality plus one SpA feature, or HLA-B27 positivity plus two SpA features. Extra-articular manifestations include acute anterior uveitis (25–40%), psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, and rarely cardiac (aortic regurgitation, conduction block) and pulmonary (apical fibrosis) involvement. NSAIDs at full anti-inflammatory dosing — continuous use in patients with active disease — is first-line therapy and may slow radiographic progression. Biological DMARDs — TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab) and IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) — are indicated for failure of two or more NSAIDs. JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are emerging alternatives.

title: Hip Fractures in the Elderly: Peri-operative Assessment and Orthogeriatric Care
red_flags: Hip fracture with cardiovascular instability pre-operatively
Peri-prosthetic fracture around hip replacement
Bilateral insufficiency fractures with severe osteoporosis
Post-surgical DVT or PE following hip fracture repair
content: Hip fractures represent a major cause of mortality, morbidity, and loss of independence in older adults, with one-year mortality rates of 20–35% and significant rates of permanent functional decline. Mayo Clinic and international guidelines emphasise that hip fractures should be considered a medical emergency requiring expedited surgical repair — ideally within 24–36 hours of admission — as delayed surgery beyond 48 hours independently increases mortality and complication rates. Hip fractures in the elderly occur predominantly at the femoral neck (intracapsular) or intertrochanteric region (extracapsular) following a low-energy fall, usually onto a hard floor. The classic presentation is inability to bear weight, shortening and external rotation of the affected limb, pain in the hip or groin, and bruising. All patients should receive immediate analgesia — femoral nerve block or fascia iliaca compartment block provides excellent pre-operative pain control and reduces opioid requirements. Cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, and cognitive assessment should be conducted simultaneously to identify and optimise comorbidities. Cardiac conditions requiring pre-operative management include AF with rate >100 bpm, heart failure, and hypo- or hyperkalaemia. Patients with dementia or delirium require modified anaesthetic and post-operative care protocols. Intracapsular fractures in fit, active patients are managed by hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty; in older, less active patients, cemented hemiarthroplasty reduces post-operative pain and revision rates compared to dynamic hip screw for displaced fractures. Intertrochanteric fractures are managed by dynamic hip screw or intramedullary nail. Post-operative orthogeriatric co-management — involving geriatric physicians in all aspects of peri-operative care — reduces mortality, delirium, and length of stay. Routine thromboprophylaxis (LMWH for 28–35 days), bone protection therapy (bisphosphonate or denosumab), and fall prevention strategies should be initiated before discharge. Rehabilitation in a designated hip fracture unit significantly improves ambulatory outcomes.

title: Tendinopathy and Tendon Rupture: Clinical Assessment and Evidence-Based Management
red_flags: Complete tendon rupture with inability to plantar flex (Achilles)
Acute tendon rupture with haemarthrosis
Spontaneous tendon rupture (fluoroquinolone-induced or on corticosteroids)
Tendinopathy with systemic inflammatory disease (RA, SpA)
content: Tendinopathy — a broad clinical term encompassing pain, swelling, and functional limitation arising from tendon pathology — is a highly prevalent musculoskeletal condition in both athletes and the general population. The contemporary understanding of tendinopathy pathophysiology has shifted from inflammatory (tendinitis) to degenerative (tendinosis) models, with focal areas of collagen fibre disorganisation, increased ground substance, neovascularity, and altered cell biology, often in the absence of classic inflammatory infiltrate. Common sites include the Achilles tendon (insertional and mid-portion), patellar tendon (jumper's knee), rotator cuff tendons (supraspinatus), common extensor origin (lateral epicondylalgia, 'tennis elbow'), common flexor origin (medial epicondylalgia), and hamstring origin at the ischial tuberosity. Risk factors include sudden increases in training load, poor lower limb biomechanics, previous injury to the same tendon, increasing age, obesity, and use of fluoroquinolone antibiotics (particularly ciprofloxacin, which inhibits collagen synthesis and can cause spontaneous rupture). The Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment (VISA) scores (VISA-A for Achilles, VISA-P for patellar) are validated tendinopathy severity tools. Load management — structured reduction followed by graduated progressive tendon loading — is the cornerstone of tendinopathy rehabilitation. The heavy slow resistance (HSR) protocol and isometric exercises (providing immediate analgesic benefit) are well-evidenced. Corticosteroid injection provides short-term pain relief but may impair long-term tendon healing and increase rupture risk with repeated use. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection has emerging evidence for certain tendinopathies (lateral epicondylalgia, patellar tendinopathy). Achilles tendon rupture — presenting with sudden onset calf pain and a palpable gap, confirmed by Thompson's test — may be managed operatively (surgical repair) or non-operatively (functional rehabilitation in a boot), with similar long-term outcomes in appropriately selected patients but higher re-rupture rate with non-operative management.

title: Paediatric Bone and Joint Disorders: Developmental Dysplasia, Perthes and SCFE
red_flags: SCFE with severe vascular compromise (acute on chronic, unstable)
Perthes disease with hip dislocation
Septic arthritis misdiagnosed as Perthes or SCFE
Hip pain in an obese adolescent with leg-length discrepancy
content: Paediatric bone and joint disorders encompass a range of developmental, vascular, and mechanical conditions that require timely recognition and specialist management to prevent long-term functional disability. Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) — previously termed congenital dislocated hip — refers to a spectrum of abnormal hip development ranging from mild acetabular dysplasia to frank dislocation. It affects 1–2 per 1,000 live births and is more common in girls, firstborns, breech presentation, and those with a family history. Neonatal screening by clinical examination (Barlow and Ortolani tests) and selective ultrasound at six weeks identifies at-risk infants. Treatment for dislocatable hips in infants under six months is Pavlik harness, maintaining hip in flexion and abduction; older infants may require closed or open reduction with spica casting. Legg-Calvé-Perthes (LCP) disease is avascular necrosis of the femoral head occurring between ages 4–8, characterised by groin or referred knee pain, antalgic gait, and limited internal rotation and abduction. MRI is the most sensitive modality for early detection of femoral head ischaemia. Treatment aims to 'contain' the femoral head within the acetabulum during the revascularisation phase: conservative management (physiotherapy, activity restriction) for mild cases; surgical containment (proximal femoral or pelvic osteotomy) for older children or severe involvement. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is the most common hip disorder in adolescents, characterised by posterior and medial displacement of the femoral head epiphysis on the metaphysis, occurring through the growth plate during the adolescent growth spurt. It most commonly affects obese male adolescents aged 11–14 years. Presentation is groin, thigh, or knee pain with an antalgic gait and limitation of hip internal rotation. X-ray (AP and frog-leg lateral views) demonstrates the classic 'ice cream falling off the cone' appearance. Unstable SCFE — where the patient cannot bear weight — is an orthopaedic emergency requiring urgent surgical fixation to prevent avascular necrosis. All SCFE are managed surgically with in-situ screw fixation. Contralateral prophylactic pinning is considered for endocrine-associated cases.

title: Toxic Shock Syndrome: Recognition, Emergency Management and Source Control
red_flags: Rapid-onset fever with hypotension and widespread erythroderma
Multiorgan failure developing over hours
TSS in menstruating woman with tampon use
Post-surgical wound infection with systemic toxicity

content: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a life-threatening, toxin-mediated systemic illness caused most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus (staphylococcal TSS, including menstrual and non-menstrual) and Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcal TSS, often associated with invasive soft tissue infection). TSS results from bacterial toxin-mediated superantigen activity, causing massive T-cell activation and cytokine release, leading to endothelial damage, capillary leak, hypotension, and multiorgan dysfunction. Staphylococcal TSS case definition requires fever above 38.9°C, diffuse macular erythroderma (sunburn-like rash), subsequent desquamation one to two weeks after onset (particularly of palms and soles), hypotension, and involvement of three or more organ systems (GI, musculoskeletal, mucous membranes, renal, haematologic, hepatic, CNS). Streptococcal TSS is characterised by hypotension with two or more of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, elevated liver enzymes, ARDS, extensive soft tissue necrosis, and erythematous rash. Emergency management requires immediate resuscitation with IV fluid boluses, vasopressors if refractory, and high-flow oxygen. Source control is critical: remove any retained foreign material (tampon, surgical packing, wound implant); debride infected or necrotic tissue urgently. IV antibiotics should be broad-spectrum and initiated immediately: flucloxacillin or cloxacillin plus clindamycin (clindamycin inhibits toxin production) for staphylococcal TSS; piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin (or meropenem in severe cases) for streptococcal TSS. MRSA coverage (vancomycin or linezolid) is added where risk is high. IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) is used in refractory streptococcal TSS to neutralise superantigens. Patients require intensive care monitoring. Clinicians should have a low threshold for recognising TSS in patients with sepsis and rash, post-operative wound infection, skin or soft tissue infection, childbirth, or menstruation.

title: Hypothyroidism and Thyroid Disorders: Diagnosis, Levothyroxine Therapy and Referral
red_flags: Myxoedema coma (hypothermia, coma, bradycardia)
New-onset thyrotoxicosis with AF and heart failure
Thyroid storm (fever, severe tachycardia, agitation)
Rapidly enlarging thyroid mass with compressive symptoms
content: Thyroid disorders are among the most prevalent endocrine conditions globally, encompassing hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) and hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid), along with structural abnormalities including goitre and thyroid nodules. Hypothyroidism affects approximately 2% of the UK population, with a prevalence up to ten times higher in women than men. Primary hypothyroidism — the most common form — results from failure of the thyroid gland itself, most commonly from autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's thyroiditis, characterised by anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies), post-radioiodine or post-surgical thyroid ablation, iodine deficiency, or drug-induced causes (amiodarone, lithium). The clinical syndrome of hypothyroidism includes fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, bradykinesia, delayed reflexes, menstrual irregularity, hypercholesterolaemia, macrocytosis, and a depressed mood. Diagnosis is by measurement of serum TSH (elevated in primary hypothyroidism) and free T4 (low or low-normal). Myxoedema coma — the most severe form, with hypothermia, severe bradycardia, decreased consciousness, and respiratory failure — requires urgent ICU management with IV liothyronine and hydrocortisone (to cover potential concurrent adrenal insufficiency), warming, and supportive care. Treatment of hypothyroidism is lifelong levothyroxine replacement, commenced at 50 mcg daily (25 mcg in elderly or ischaemic heart disease patients) and titrated to normalise TSH within the reference range (0.4–4.0 mIU/L). Hyperthyroidism, most commonly due to Graves' disease (TSH receptor autoantibody-driven diffuse toxic goitre), is treated with antithyroid drugs (carbimazole or propylthiouracil), radioiodine therapy, or thyroidectomy. Thyroid storm — a life-threatening hyperthyroid emergency — is managed with IV beta-blockers, antithyroid drugs, iodine solution, corticosteroids, and supportive care. All patients with thyroid nodules should undergo thyroid ultrasound and risk stratification with TSH measurement; fine-needle aspiration cytology is indicated for nodules with suspicious sonographic features.

title: Erythroderma: Emergency Assessment, Differential Diagnosis and Management
red_flags: Erythroderma with cardiovascular instability (high-output cardiac failure)
Erythroderma with fever and positive blood cultures (sepsis)
Erythroderma with blistering (TEN, pemphigus)
New erythroderma with lymphadenopathy (lymphoma, Sézary syndrome)
content: Erythroderma (exfoliative dermatitis) is a severe, potentially life-threatening inflammatory skin condition defined by generalised redness and scaling affecting more than 90% of the body surface area. It carries significant morbidity from disruption of the skin barrier — including temperature dysregulation, high-output cardiac failure (from massively increased cutaneous blood flow), hypoalbuminaemia, protein loss through exfoliation, electrolyte disturbances, and secondary bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes). Mortality ranges from 1.4 to 14% and is highest in elderly patients and those with underlying haematological malignancy. The principal causes in adults include pre-existing inflammatory dermatoses (psoriasis — the most common — eczema/atopic dermatitis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact dermatitis), drug reactions (allopurinol, sulfonamides, antiepileptics, gold, penicillins — may occur weeks after initiation), cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides and its leukaemic variant Sézary syndrome), and idiopathic (up to 25% of cases). Less common causes include pemphigus foliaceus, toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), pityriasis rubra pilaris, and Norwegian (crusted) scabies. All patients with erythroderma require hospitalisation for monitoring and supportive care: temperature regulation (warm environment), fluid and electrolyte replacement, nutritional support with high-protein diet or supplementation, emollients applied frequently to restore barrier function, and thromboprophylaxis (risk of DVT from immobility and hypercoagulable state). Specific treatment depends on the aetiology: systemic corticosteroids or ciclosporin for inflammatory dermatoses; identification and withdrawal of the causative drug for drug-induced cases; systemic retinoids or methotrexate for psoriatic erythroderma; PUVA, bexarotene, extracorporeal photopheresis, or biological therapy for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Skin biopsy — multiple biopsies from different sites — is essential to establish the diagnosis histologically and exclude lymphoma.

title: Fever of Unknown Origin: Systematic Investigation and Referral
red_flags: Fever with marked weight loss (malignancy or TB)
Fever with hepatosplenomegaly and cytopaenia (lymphoma or visceral leishmaniasis)
Fever with new cardiac murmur (endocarditis)
Fever with progressive confusion (encephalitis or CNS lymphoma)
content: Fever of unknown origin (FUO) is defined as a temperature greater than 38.3°C (101°F) on multiple occasions, illness lasting more than three weeks, and failure to establish a diagnosis despite one week of appropriate investigation in hospital or three outpatient visits. This classic definition (Petersdorf and Beeson, 1961) encompasses a broad spectrum of diagnostic possibilities and demands a methodical, systematic approach. FUO is most commonly caused by: infections (25–40%, including infective endocarditis, tuberculosis, intraabdominal abscess, CMV, EBV, HIV, brucellosis, Q fever, typhoid, and visceral leishmaniasis in endemic areas); malignancy (20–30%, particularly lymphoma, leukaemia, renal cell carcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma); and inflammatory/autoimmune diseases (15–25%, including adult-onset Still's disease, vasculitis, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, sarcoidosis, and inflammatory bowel disease); with a small proportion remaining undiagnosed (10–15%). Clinical assessment should include a meticulous history (travel history, animal contact, occupational exposure, sexual history, medication review, family history, prior medical conditions) and comprehensive physical examination (lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, joint examination, heart murmur, fundoscopy). First-line investigations include FBC, ESR, CRP, procalcitonin, LFTs, U&E, LDH, uric acid, protein electrophoresis, three sets of blood cultures, urine culture, viral serology (CMV, EBV, HIV), ANA, ANCA, RF, immunoglobulins, TSH, CXR, echocardiography, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and bone marrow biopsy when haematological malignancy is suspected. PET-CT has significantly improved the diagnostic yield in FUO by identifying malignancy, vasculitis, and occult infection. Empirical antibiotics, antifungals, or corticosteroids should be avoided until a diagnosis is established, as they may mask treatable conditions. Referral to infectious diseases and internal medicine is recommended for all patients meeting FUO criteria.

title: Vitamin D Deficiency: Prevalence, Clinical Features, Supplementation and Monitoring
red_flags: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany or seizures
Severe vitamin D deficiency with osteomalacia and pathological fractures
Vitamin D deficiency with malabsorption syndrome
Persistent severe deficiency despite adequate supplementation
content: Vitamin D deficiency is a highly prevalent global health problem, affecting an estimated 1 billion people worldwide, including 20–50% of the UK adult population. Vitamin D — a fat-soluble pro-hormone synthesised in the skin upon ultraviolet B radiation exposure or obtained through dietary sources and supplements — is essential for calcium absorption, bone mineralisation, immune regulation, neuromuscular function, and cardiovascular health. Vitamin D status is measured by serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OHD) concentration: deficiency is defined as <25 nmol/L (<10 ng/mL); insufficiency as 25–50 nmol/L; sufficiency as >50 nmol/L (>20 ng/mL). Risk groups for deficiency include individuals with dark skin pigmentation, those who are housebound or institutionalised, individuals who cover most of their skin for religious or cultural reasons, obese individuals (vitamin D is sequestered in adipose tissue), patients with malabsorption syndromes (coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, bariatric surgery), those with chronic liver or kidney disease, and exclusively breastfed infants. Clinical manifestations of severe deficiency include osteomalacia (bone pain, muscle weakness, proximal myopathy, and pathological fractures) in adults, and rickets (impaired bone mineralisation, bowing of limbs, craniotabes, and growth retardation) in children. Symptomatic hypocalcaemia — perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, and seizures — may complicate profound deficiency. NHS guidance recommends universal supplementation for high-risk groups: 10 mcg (400 IU) daily throughout the year. For confirmed deficiency, loading regimens — 50,000 IU weekly for 6–10 weeks (colecalciferol D3) — are used followed by maintenance 800–2000 IU daily. All supplementation should be with vitamin D3 (colecalciferol) rather than D2 (ergocalciferol), which is less bioavailable. Monitoring with 25-OHD levels is recommended 3–6 months after commencing supplementation and annually thereafter in high-risk patients.

title: Anaphylaxis: Recognition, Emergency Treatment and Allergen Investigation
red_flags: Anaphylaxis with stridor or severe bronchospasm
Cardiovascular collapse within seconds of allergen exposure
Refractory anaphylaxis unresponsive to epinephrine
Biphasic anaphylaxis (recurrence 1–72 hours after initial reaction)
content: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening, generalised or systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterised by rapid onset of airway compromise, breathing difficulty, cardiovascular collapse, and/or mucocutaneous features. It represents an IgE-mediated immune response (or non-IgE mechanisms in certain cases) to allergens including foods (peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, fish, milk, egg), drugs (penicillin, NSAIDs, contrast media), insect venom, latex, and exercise-triggered reactions. Recognition requires a high index of suspicion: anaphylaxis is likely if there is acute onset (minutes to hours) with involvement of the skin or mucosal tissue (urticaria, angioedema, flushing, pruritus), combined with either respiratory compromise (dyspnoea, wheeze, stridor, reduced SpO2) or cardiovascular collapse (hypotension, collapse, syncope), or persistent GI symptoms after allergen exposure in a patient with known food allergy. Immediate treatment is intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) 0.5 mg (500 mcg) for adults, 0.3 mg (300 mcg) for children 6–12 years, administered into the anterolateral thigh — the most reliably absorbed injection site — using an auto-injector or syringe. Adrenaline is the only life-saving treatment and must not be delayed. Patients should be positioned supine (or recovery position if unconscious); those with respiratory distress may prefer sitting. IV fluid resuscitation with 500–1000 mL crystalloid bolus addresses vasodilatory hypotension. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are secondary adjunct treatments and do not replace adrenaline. All patients require hospital observation for a minimum of four to six hours (or 12 hours for severe reactions) to monitor for biphasic anaphylaxis. Following recovery, patients should be prescribed two epinephrine auto-injectors, receive anaphylaxis action plan documentation, and be referred to a specialist allergy clinic for allergen identification, specific IgE and skin prick testing, and long-term management including allergen immunotherapy where available.

title: Sepsis: Recognition, Six-Hour Bundle and Source Identification
red_flags: Septic shock (MAP <65 mmHg unresponsive to fluids)
Lactate >4 mmol/L
New organ dysfunction (AKI, coagulopathy, altered consciousness)
Sepsis in immunocompromised or neutropenic patient
content: Sepsis is defined as a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is a subset with circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormalities sufficiently severe to substantially increase mortality, defined clinically by the need for vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 65 mmHg or above, with a serum lactate greater than 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Sepsis-3 definitions (Sepsis-3, Singer et al., JAMA 2016) have replaced the SIRS-based criteria with organ dysfunction assessment using the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, with an acute increase of 2 or more SOFA points indicating sepsis. The quick SOFA (qSOFA) — altered mentation, respiratory rate ≥22, systolic BP ≤100 — is a rapid bedside screening tool. Early clinical suspicion is essential: any patient with infection and organ dysfunction, unexplained confusion, tachycardia, tachypnoea, or hypotension should be considered to have sepsis until proven otherwise. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle mandates: (1) measure lactate; re-measure if initial >2 mmol/L; (2) obtain blood cultures before antibiotics; (3) administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within one hour of sepsis recognition; (4) administer 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension (MAP <65 mmHg) or lactate ≥4 mmol/L; (5) apply vasopressors (noradrenaline/norepinephrine as first-line) for hypotension during or after resuscitation to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg. NHS NICE guidance (NG51) stratifies patients into low, moderate, and high risk of sepsis with specific time-to-treatment targets. Source identification and control — imaging (chest X-ray, CT), urine culture, wound assessment, and removal of indwelling devices — is a critical parallel priority. Broad-spectrum antibiotic de-escalation, guided by microbiology results, should occur within 48–72 hours to reduce antimicrobial resistance. Patients meeting septic shock criteria require ICU admission for haemodynamic monitoring, organ support, and advanced care.

title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Clinical Features, Flare Management and Renal Involvement
red_flags: Lupus nephritis with rapidly rising creatinine (proliferative)
Acute neuropsychiatric lupus (psychosis, seizures)
Lupus with severe thrombocytopaenia (<20 × 10⁹/L)
Acute serositis with haemodynamic compromise
content: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic, multisystem autoimmune disease characterised by immune complex deposition, complement activation, and widespread organ inflammation. It disproportionately affects women of reproductive age (female-to-male ratio 9:1), with higher prevalence and more severe disease in Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic, and Asian populations. The clinical manifestations of SLE are highly variable and may involve virtually any organ system, most commonly the musculoskeletal system (arthralgia, non-erosive arthritis — 95%), skin (malar or butterfly rash, discoid lupus, photosensitivity, oral ulcers — 85%), kidneys (lupus nephritis — 50%), cardiovascular system (pericarditis, myocarditis, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, accelerated atherosclerosis), nervous system (headache, cognitive dysfunction, psychosis, seizures, stroke — neuropsychiatric SLE), haematological system (haemolytic anaemia, lymphopaenia, thrombocytopaenia), and serositis (pleuritis, pericarditis). The 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria score patients on clinical domains and immunological findings (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm antibodies, complement C3/C4). ANA positivity (titre ≥1:80) with high-titre anti-dsDNA and low complement is characteristic during active disease. The SLEDAI-2K score quantifies disease activity and guides treatment decisions. Lupus nephritis (LN) — a major cause of morbidity — is classified by the ISN/RPS histological system (class I–VI); class III and IV (proliferative LN) have the highest risk of end-stage renal disease and require aggressive immunosuppression: high-dose corticosteroids combined with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) or IV cyclophosphamide for induction, followed by MMF or azathioprine for maintenance. Hydroxychloroquine is recommended for all SLE patients without contraindication, reducing flares, organ damage, and thrombotic risk. Belimumab (anti-BLYS monoclonal antibody) and voclosporin are approved add-on therapies for active LN and extrenal manifestations. NSAID use should be minimised due to renal and cardiovascular risk.

title: Malaria: Global Diagnosis, Treatment Protocols and Severe Disease Management
red_flags: Cerebral malaria (impaired consciousness, seizures, coma)
Severe malaria with respiratory distress or pulmonary oedema
Hyperparasitaemia (>5% infected RBCs)
Malaria in pregnancy (risk of placental malaria and fetal loss)
content: Malaria is a life-threatening parasitic disease caused by Plasmodium species transmitted through the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. It remains one of the most significant global health challenges, with an estimated 249 million cases and 608,000 deaths worldwide in 2022, the majority in sub-Saharan Africa and predominantly in children under five years. Five Plasmodium species infect humans: P. falciparum (most virulent, predominant in Africa and responsible for severe malaria), P. vivax (most geographically widespread), P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi. WHO guidelines classify malaria as uncomplicated or severe. Severe malaria — defined by WHO as proven or suspected malaria with one or more of the following: impaired consciousness, prostration, respiratory distress, circulatory collapse, abnormal bleeding, jaundice with vital organ dysfunction, haemoglobinuria, hyperparasitaemia (>5% parasitised RBCs), hypoglycaemia, or severe anaemia (Hb <5 g/dL) — carries mortality of 10–50% without prompt treatment. Diagnosis requires confirmation by microscopy (thick and thin blood films — gold standard), or rapid diagnostic test (RDT detecting P. falciparum histidine-rich protein-2 or other antigens) when microscopy is not immediately available. PCR is the most sensitive method but not point-of-care. Treatment of uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria: artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) — artemether-lumefantrine or artesunate-amodiaquine — is WHO first-line; partial artemisinin resistance in Southeast Asia necessitates longer courses and partner drug adaptation. Severe malaria: IV or IM artesunate is superior to quinine and is first-line; IV quinine is an alternative when artesunate is unavailable. Hypoglycaemia (a complication of both severe malaria and quinine treatment) must be monitored and corrected. P. vivax and P. ovale carry hepatic hypnozoites requiring primaquine (after G6PD testing) for radical cure to prevent relapse. Malaria in pregnancy requires specialist management and ACT with specific safety profiles. Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is recommended in areas of high transmission.

title: Typhoid Fever: Diagnosis, Antimicrobial Treatment and Outbreak Control
red_flags: Intestinal perforation with peritonitis
Severe haemorrhage from intestinal ulcers
Typhoid encephalopathy with altered consciousness
Septic shock with typhoid
content: Typhoid fever is a systemic infection caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (typhoid) and, to a lesser extent, S. Paratyphi (paratyphoid fever), transmitted by the faecal-oral route through contaminated food or water. The WHO estimates approximately 11–21 million cases annually, with over 150,000 deaths, occurring predominantly in South Asia, Africa, and Southeast Asia. The classic clinical syndrome evolves over three to four weeks: fever increasing in a step-wise pattern reaching 39–40°C, associated with relative bradycardia (pulse-temperature dissociation), headache, malaise, anorexia, and abdominal pain. Rose spots — faint, salmon-coloured maculopapular lesions on the trunk — are a classic but transient and easily missed sign. Diarrhoea occurs in some patients, while constipation is more common early in the course. The third week carries the risk of intestinal perforation (1–3% of cases) and haemorrhage from Peyer's patches ulceration — presenting with sudden worsening abdominal pain, rigidity, and signs of peritonism. Hepatosplenomegaly is frequently found. Blood culture (sensitivity 60–80%) is the gold standard diagnostic method in the first week. Bone marrow culture (sensitivity >90%) is more sensitive and remains positive after antibiotic treatment has started. The Widal test has poor sensitivity and specificity and should not be used for diagnosis. Stool and urine cultures become positive from the second week. Treatment: WHO recommends fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin) for susceptible strains; however, extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid — first emerging in Pakistan in 2016 and spreading to other countries — is resistant to fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, and ampicillin, leaving azithromycin as the oral option and carbapenems for severe disease. Travel history to endemic areas and antibiogram results must inform antibiotic selection. Surgical consultation is required for intestinal perforation. Vaccination with Vi polysaccharide vaccine or Ty21a oral vaccine is recommended for travellers and endemic-area populations.

title: Dengue Fever: Clinical Grading, Warning Signs and Management Protocol
red_flags: Dengue with warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation)
Dengue haemorrhagic fever with shock (DSS)
Platelet count <20,000 with spontaneous bleeding
Severe dengue with organ impairment (hepatitis, encephalitis, myocarditis)
content: Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne viral disease caused by four dengue virus serotypes (DENV 1–4), transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. It is the most rapidly spreading vector-borne disease globally, with an estimated 100–400 million infections annually across approximately 128 countries, predominantly in tropical and subtropical regions of Asia, Latin America, and Africa. The WHO 2009 dengue classification divides dengue into: dengue without warning signs, dengue with warning signs, and severe dengue. Dengue typically presents with sudden-onset high fever (39–40°C) lasting 2–7 days, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia and arthralgia ('breakbone fever'), nausea, vomiting, and a rash (initially diffuse maculopapular, evolving to petechiae in later stages). The critical phase — occurring around defervescence (days 4–6 of illness) — is when complications arise from plasma leakage, haemorrhage, and severe organ impairment. Warning signs of disease progression include abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion), mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver enlargement >2 cm, and rising haematocrit with rapid decrease in platelet count. Dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS) represent severe plasma leakage and circulatory compromise requiring immediate IV fluid resuscitation. Diagnosis: dengue NS1 antigen detection (days 1–5 of illness), dengue IgM/IgG serology (from day 4), and RT-PCR for serotyping. No specific antiviral therapy is available; management is supportive. IV fluid therapy (IV isotonic crystalloids at carefully titrated rates) is the cornerstone for severe dengue; excessive fluid can cause pulmonary oedema. Platelet transfusion is reserved for active serious bleeding with severe thrombocytopaenia. Aspirin and NSAIDs are contraindicated due to bleeding risk and risk of Reye's syndrome in children; paracetamol is the analgesic of choice. All patients with warning signs should be hospitalised for monitoring and management.

title: HIV/AIDS: Global Testing Guidance, Antiretroviral Therapy and Opportunistic Infection Management
red_flags: PCP pneumonia with respiratory failure (AIDS-defining)
Cryptococcal meningitis (AIDS-defining)
Toxoplasma encephalitis with ring-enhancing lesions
Severe wasting with CD4 <50 cells/µL
content: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection remains a global pandemic, with approximately 39 million people living with HIV globally in 2022, the majority in sub-Saharan Africa. The WHO 'Treat All' strategy recommends initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for all people living with HIV regardless of CD4 cell count, as early treatment reduces transmission, AIDS-defining events, and HIV-associated non-AIDS conditions including cardiovascular disease, malignancy, and neurocognitive impairment. HIV destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes, progressively impairing cellular immunity. Untreated, the median time from infection to AIDS is 10 years. AIDS is defined by a CD4 count below 200 cells/µL or the presence of an AIDS-defining illness. WHO clinical staging classifies HIV disease into stages 1–4 based on clinical events, guiding treatment initiation and prophylaxis decisions. Recommended first-line ART regimens comprise two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) — tenofovir alafenamide or disoproxil fumarate plus lamivudine or emtricitabine — combined with an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI: dolutegravir or bictegravir). Dolutegravir-based regimens are preferred globally for their high genetic barrier to resistance, tolerability, and low pill burden. Viral load monitoring and CD4 count guide treatment response and immunological recovery. Opportunistic infection (OI) prophylaxis is based on CD4 thresholds: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) and toxoplasmosis prevention (CD4 <200 cells/µL); azithromycin for Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) prophylaxis (CD4 <50 cells/µL). Cryptococcal meningitis — presenting with headache, fever, and meningism in patients with CD4 <100 — requires CSF India ink preparation, cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) testing, and antifungal induction therapy with amphotericin B plus flucytosine. The immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) — paradoxical worsening of OI symptoms after ART initiation — occurs in 10–30% of patients and is managed with corticosteroids in severe cases.

title: Meningococcal Disease: Emergency Recognition, Prophylaxis and Vaccination
red_flags: Non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash with fever
Meningococcal disease with fulminant purpura fulminans
Septic shock within hours of initial symptoms
Household contact of confirmed meningococcal case
content: Invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) caused by Neisseria meningitidis is one of the most rapidly fatal bacterial infections, with the capacity to progress from a well-appearing child to death within 24 hours if unrecognised. Thirteen serogroups of N. meningitidis are identified, with serogroups B, C, W, and Y responsible for the majority of disease in high-income countries, and serogroup A predominating in the African meningitis belt. The clinical presentation encompasses two main syndromes: meningitis (fever, headache, photophobia, phonophobia, neck stiffness, vomiting) and meningococcal septicaemia (bacteraemia without meningitis), which is associated with higher mortality. The hallmark of meningococcal septicaemia is a rapidly spreading, non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash reflecting meningococcal bacteraemia and cutaneous infarction — this rash does NOT blanch under pressure (glass test) and distinguishes IMD from benign causes of petechiae. Purpura fulminans — extensive cutaneous haemorrhage and necrosis with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) — represents the most severe form with mortality exceeding 40%. Early recognition is critical: initiation of parenteral benzylpenicillin (or ceftriaxone in penicillin allergy) by the first healthcare professional in contact — before hospital admission — is associated with improved survival. This recommendation does not require laboratory confirmation. Emergency management in hospital includes immediate blood cultures, IV ceftriaxone 2 g (100 mg/kg in children), aggressive fluid resuscitation for septic shock, vasopressors, corticosteroids (controversial in meningococcal septicaemia but used in confirmed meningitis), and ICU admission. Chemoprophylaxis with ciprofloxacin or rifampicin is mandatory for close household contacts within 24 hours of case identification. Vaccination programmes: MenB vaccine (Bexsero) for infants and adolescents; MenACWY for adolescents and travellers; meningococcal A conjugate vaccine for sub-Saharan Africa. School and university outbreaks require public health coordination.

title: Diabetes-Related Emergencies: Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Hyperosmolar State
red_flags: Severe acidosis (pH <7.1) with impaired consciousness
HHS with serum osmolality >340 mOsm/kg
DKA with concurrent sepsis or acute MI (precipitant)
Cerebral oedema during DKA treatment (paediatric)
content: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) are the two major life-threatening metabolic emergencies of diabetes mellitus, requiring prompt recognition, systematic investigation, and evidence-based treatment protocols. DKA occurs predominantly in type 1 diabetes but is increasingly recognised in type 2 diabetes (particularly with SGLT2 inhibitor use, euglycaemic DKA). It results from insulin deficiency combined with elevated counter-regulatory hormones, leading to unchecked lipolysis, ketogenesis (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate, acetone), metabolic acidosis, osmotic diuresis, and profound dehydration. DKA diagnostic criteria: blood glucose >11 mmol/L (or known diabetes), ketonaemia >3 mmol/L or significant ketonuria (≥2+ on dipstick), and bicarbonate <15 mmol/L or venous pH <7.3. Severity is classified as mild (venous pH 7.25–7.30), moderate (7.0–7.25), or severe (<7.0). Common precipitants include new-onset type 1 diabetes, infection (most common), insulin omission, myocardial infarction, and drugs (SGLT2 inhibitors). The clinical presentation includes polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing (deep, rapid compensatory breathing for metabolic acidosis), and in severe cases, reduced consciousness. HHS occurs in type 2 diabetes, characterised by profound hyperglycaemia (glucose >30 mmol/L), severe hyperosmolarity (effective osmolarity >320 mOsm/kg), and dehydration without significant ketosis or acidosis. Marked neurological features (confusion, coma, focal deficit) are more pronounced in HHS than DKA. Treatment of DKA follows the Joint British Diabetes Societies (JBDS) protocol: IV 0.9% sodium chloride fluid resuscitation (1 L over 1 hour, then 1 L over 2 hours, then 1 L over 4 hours), fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (0.1 units/kg/hour) commenced once potassium >3.5 mmol/L, potassium replacement in infusion bags, glucose monitoring every hour, ketonaemia monitoring every 1–2 hours, and transition to subcutaneous insulin once DKA is resolved. Cerebral oedema — a rare but catastrophic complication of DKA treatment in children — presents with headache, confusion, bradycardia, and hypertension, requiring immediate IV mannitol or hypertonic saline.

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease and Extraintestinal Manifestations: Systemic Considerations
red_flags: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with bacterial cholangitis
Acute anterior uveitis with untreated IBD
Severe erythema nodosum with fulminant colitis
Deep vein thrombosis in active IBD (hypercoagulable state)
content: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) — comprising Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis — is a systemic condition with extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) occurring in approximately 50% of patients, frequently preceding, accompanying, or occurring independent of bowel disease activity. Recognition of EIMs is clinically important as they may be the presenting complaint, signal disease flare, require specific treatment, or indicate the need for IBD treatment escalation. EIMs are categorised by their relationship to intestinal disease activity: those that parallel gut activity — peripheral arthropathy (type 1: large-joint, pauciarticular; most commonly colitis-related), oral ulceration (aphthous ulcers), and erythema nodosum (painful, tender nodules on the anterior shins) — usually respond to treatment of the underlying IBD. Those independent of IBD activity include type 2 peripheral arthropathy (small-joint polyarthritis), axial spondyloarthropathy (sacroiliitis, ankylosing spondylitis), uveitis (anterior or intermediate), primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), and pyoderma gangrenosum. Anterior uveitis in IBD requires urgent ophthalmological assessment as corneal scarring and visual loss may result without prompt treatment (topical and systemic corticosteroids). PSC — chronic fibro-inflammatory biliary stricturing — occurs in 5% of UC patients and is associated with significantly increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer; management requires ERCP for biliary intervention and consideration of liver transplantation in advanced cases. IBD is associated with a two-to-threefold increased risk of venous thromboembolism, particularly during active disease; thromboprophylaxis should be administered to all hospitalised IBD patients. Mayo Clinic guidelines emphasise the importance of close collaboration between gastroenterologists, rheumatologists, ophthalmologists, and dermatologists in the management of patients with EIMs. Treatment of systemic EIMs may require biological therapy (anti-TNF agents, ustekinumab) targeting both intestinal and extraintestinal disease simultaneously.

title: Adrenal Insufficiency and Addisonian Crisis: Recognition and Emergency Treatment
red_flags: Hypotension with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia (Addisonian crisis)
Altered consciousness in a patient on long-term corticosteroids
Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen)
Hypoglycaemia with features of adrenal insufficiency
content: Adrenal insufficiency (AI) is caused by impaired production of cortisol and, in primary AI, aldosterone. It may be primary (Addison's disease — adrenal cortex destruction, most commonly autoimmune in developed countries, or TB adrenalitis in developing countries), secondary (pituitary failure — ACTH deficiency), or tertiary (hypothalamic failure — CRH deficiency, most commonly from exogenous corticosteroid suppression). Addisonian crisis — acute AI — is a medical emergency with potential for death if not recognised and treated immediately. Precipitants include intercurrent illness, surgery, trauma, medication omission, or bilateral adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome — catastrophic adrenal haemorrhage, classically associated with meningococcal septicaemia and presenting with purpuric rash, cardiovascular collapse, and death). Clinical features of Addisonian crisis include severe hypotension (may progress to shock), abdominal pain mimicking a surgical abdomen, nausea and vomiting, confusion or reduced consciousness, and hyperpyrexia. Biochemical hallmarks include hyponatraemia (dilutional, from ADH excess and lack of free-water clearance), hyperkalaemia (from aldosterone deficiency in primary AI), and hypoglycaemia. Hyperpigmentation (generalised, particularly in skin creases, buccal mucosa, and old scars) is a clinical sign specific to primary AI, resulting from elevated ACTH and MSH driving melanocyte stimulation. Emergency treatment must not be delayed for diagnostic confirmation: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately, followed by 100 mg every 6–8 hours for 24 hours, alongside aggressive IV 0.9% saline fluid resuscitation. Blood glucose monitoring with IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia. Once clinically stable, hydrocortisone is tapered to oral replacement dosing (15–25 mg/day in divided doses) and fludrocortisone (0.1 mg daily) is added for primary AI to replace mineralocorticoid activity. All patients with AI require sick day rules education — doubling oral hydrocortisone during illness — and should wear a medical alert bracelet. Emergency hydrocortisone injection kits (100 mg IM hydrocortisone) should be prescribed and patients trained in self-administration.
